# How to use this guide

Experimental Pharmacology (BP810ET) is a Semester 8 elective worth 3 theory credits. Coming at the end of the B.Pharm programme, it expects you to already know receptor pharmacology, biochemistry, and the major drug classes from Pharmacology I, II and III. What it adds is the **experimental dimension**: how pharmacologists actually measure drug activity, test safety and develop a PK profile before a drug reaches clinical trials. These skills are directly relevant to careers in pharmaceutical R&D, regulatory affairs and academic research.

There is no practical paper for this elective in the standard PCI scheme, so all learning is examined in writing. The marks come from: understanding the **principles** and **calculations** of bioassay, knowing the **animal models** in detail (purpose, procedure, endpoint, control drug), and applying **toxicological and pharmacokinetic concepts** to drug development scenarios.

## Exam pattern

| Section | What it asks | Marks |
| --- | --- | --- |
| A | 20 objective / MCQ questions (attempt all) | 20 × 1 = 20 |
| B | Long essays — attempt 2 of 3 | 2 × 10 = 20 |
| C | Short answers — attempt 7 of 9 | 7 × 5 = 35 |

**Total: 75 marks, 180 minutes.** Confirm the exact paper pattern with your college, as universities may vary Section B and C counts.

## Unit-by-unit syllabus mapping

| Unit | Topics in these notes | Likely exam weight |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 Principles and Ethics of Bioassay | Types of bioassay, standards, dose-response curves, 3-point and 4-point methods, probit analysis, LD50, index of precision, validity tests, 3Rs, CPCSEA, randomisation | High |
| 2 Isolated Tissue Bioassays | Organ bath components, Krebs solution, isolated tissue preparations table, four-point assay calculation, pA2 / Schild plot | High |
| 3 Autacoid Bioassays | Properties and bioassay of histamine, 5-HT, bradykinin, angiotensin, prostaglandins, ACh; in-vitro vs in-vivo; cascade superfusion | Medium–High |
| 4 CNS / Anti-inflammatory / Analgesic Screening | Actophotometer, sleeping time, rotarod, EPM, FST, MES, PTZ; carrageenan, cotton pellet, writhing, formalin, hot plate | High |
| 5 Toxicity Studies and PK | Lorke's LD50, sub-acute study parameters, NOAEL, Ames test, micronucleus, ICH S guidelines, PK parameter calculation, allometric scaling, drug discovery pipeline | Medium–High |

## Probability ratings

- **High** — asked in most sittings of this elective; know the full answer with procedures, calculations and reference drugs.
- **Medium** — appears every few years or as part of a broader question.
- **Low** — rare; useful for the MCQ section.

## High-probability topics to know cold

1. **3Rs and CPCSEA** — definitions with examples; IAEC composition; humane endpoints.
2. **Dose-response curve and bioassay calculation** — log-dose vs response, slope, interpolation, four-point parallel-line assay calculation, index of precision λ, validity tests.
3. **Isolated guinea pig ileum** — preparation, what it detects, receptor types, Schultz-Dale reaction.
4. **Carrageenan paw oedema** — phases with mediators, plethysmometry, % inhibition calculation, reference drug.
5. **Acetic acid writhing test** — procedure, opioids vs NSAIDs comparison, sensitivity vs selectivity.
6. **Lorke's LD50 method** — stage 1 and stage 2 animal numbers, calculation formula.
7. **PK parameter calculation** — AUC by trapezoidal rule, CL, Vd, t½, bioavailability.
8. **ICH toxicity guidelines** — categories Q, S, E; specific S-series guidelines for genotoxicity, reproductive toxicity, repeat-dose.
9. **Formalin test phases** — Phase 1 (neurogenic, opioid-sensitive) vs Phase 2 (inflammatory, NSAID-sensitive).
10. **Four-point parallel-line assay** — why parallelism matters, what it means if slopes differ.

## Scoring tips for this subject

1. **Draw a labelled diagram for the organ bath in every question that involves an isolated tissue preparation.** A clean diagram with the labels (jacketed bath, Krebs solution, gas inlet, transducer, tissue hooks, drain tap) earns one to two marks and signals that you understand the setup. Even a rough sketch is better than no diagram.

2. **Write a worked calculation step by step.** In bioassay questions (three-point assay, interpolation, AUC, bioavailability) the examiner awards marks for the method and each step, not just the final number. Write out the formula, substitute values, show the arithmetic.

3. **State the reference drug and the direction of change.** For every screening model answer, say which reference drug you are comparing with and whether the endpoint increases or decreases. For example: "Morphine at 5 mg/kg i.p. increased the tail-flick latency from 3 s (vehicle) to 9 s; the test compound at 10 mg/kg increased it to 7 s, suggesting moderate central analgesic activity."

4. **Classify before you describe.** In a question on toxicity studies or bioassay types, start with a classification (quantal vs graded, in-vitro vs in-vivo, acute vs sub-acute vs chronic) and then discuss each class. Examiners count the classes and their examples.

5. **Distinguish similar-sounding models precisely.** The tail flick test and the hot plate test both use thermal stimuli, but the tail flick is a spinal reflex and the hot plate is supraspinal — write this distinction explicitly. The MES test and PTZ test both screen antiepileptics, but they predict different seizure types — state which is which.

6. **In ethics questions, use the exact terminology.** Replacement, Reduction and Refinement are capitalised. CPCSEA is not just "an animal ethics body" — it operates under the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals Act, 1960, and requires an IAEC with a specified composition.

7. **Link PK to dose design.** When you write about PK parameter calculation, finish with one sentence connecting NOAEL or AUC to what it means for clinical dose selection or for the drug discovery pipeline.

# Last-night revision sheet

Focus your final hour on five answers: **the matched-dose bioassay method (calculations + diagram)**, **Schultz-Dale technique and sensitisation for anaphylaxis**, **hot-plate vs tail-flick for analgesic screening**, **LD₅₀ and therapeutic index calculations**, and **the three classic autacoid bioassays (histamine, 5-HT, acetylcholine) with their standard preparations**. These cover the core 10-mark questions.

---

## Definitions in one line

| Term | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| Bioassay | Estimation of potency or activity of a substance using a living organism or its parts |
| Standardisation | Matching the potency of a preparation to that of a standard |
| Sensitivity | Smallest dose that produces a detectable response |
| Specificity | Ability to detect one substance in a mixture |
| Precision | Reproducibility of repeated estimates |
| ED₅₀ | Dose producing the desired effect in 50% of animals |
| LD₅₀ | Dose lethal to 50% of animals |
| Therapeutic index | LD₅₀ ÷ ED₅₀ (wider = safer) |
| Graded response | Response varies continuously with dose |
| Quantal response | All-or-none; each animal either responds or does not |
| Peristaltic wave | Coordinate contraction-relaxation wave used in guinea-pig ileum |
| Sensitisation | Pre-exposure to antigen causing IgE-mediated mast cell priming |
| In-vivo model | Experiment in a living whole animal |
| In-vitro model | Experiment in isolated organ, cell or tissue |

---

## Standard bioassay preparations — at a glance

| Autacoid | Preparation | Contraction or relaxation? | Species |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Histamine | Guinea-pig ileum (Mg-free Tyrode) | Contraction | Guinea pig |
| Histamine (alternate) | Rat uterus | Contraction | Rat |
| 5-HT (serotonin) | Rat fundal strip | Contraction | Rat |
| 5-HT (alternate) | Rabbit ear artery | Contraction (5-HT₂) | Rabbit |
| Acetylcholine | Frog rectus abdominis | Contraction | Frog |
| Acetylcholine (alternate) | Leech dorsal muscle | Contraction | Leech |
| Bradykinin | Rat uterus (oestrogen-primed) | Contraction | Rat |
| Angiotensin II | Rat aortic strip | Contraction | Rat |

---

## Bioassay methods — when to use each

| Method | Use when | Key calculation |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Three-point (3+3) | Routine potency estimate; most common exam answer | 2 test doses + 2 std doses; use log-dose scale |
| Four-point (2+2) | High precision needed | 2 std + 2 test on same preparation |
| Multiple-point | Research settings; more doses | Dose-response curve, interpolation |
| Bracket dilution | Approximate estimate quickly | Straddle the standard response |

---

## Matched-dose (2+2) bioassay steps

```text
1. Mount preparation; allow to equilibrate (30 min).
2. Prepare dose-response curve for the standard (S1, S2 — two doses, e.g. 1 and 2 µg/mL).
3. Confirm linearity and parallelism.
4. Apply test doses (T1, T2) to bracket the standard responses.
5. Interpolate on the log-dose axis: M = log(T) − log(S) for matched responses.
6. Potency ratio = antilog(M); multiply by concentration of standard.
7. Report with confidence limits.
```

---

## Schultz-Dale technique (anaphylaxis bioassay)

```text
Sensitisation phase (10–14 days before):
  Guinea pig ← inject antigen (ovalbumin) IP or SC.
  IgE forms, sensitises mast cells in smooth muscle.

Assay day:
  Isolate guinea-pig ileum; mount in organ bath (Tyrode at 37°C, O₂).
  Add antigen (ovalbumin) → antigen + IgE on mast cells → degranulation
  → Histamine + other mediators released locally
  → Brisk, immediate contraction of the ileum.
```

**Measurement**: height of contraction = index of anaphylaxis. Antihistamines inhibit the response. Used to test antiallergic drugs.

---

## Analgesic screening models — comparison

| Model | Stimulus | Endpoint | Opioids | NSAIDs | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Hot plate | Thermal (55°C plate) | Latency to lick paw or jump | Yes | Weak | Supraspinal; can be adapted |
| Tail flick (D'Amour & Smith) | Radiant heat beam on tail | Tail withdrawal latency | Yes | Poor | Spinal reflex; objective |
| Acetic acid writhing | Chemical (IP acetic acid) | Number of writhes in 20 min | Yes | Yes (better) | Sensitive to both; screen first |
| Formalin test | Chemical (SC formalin) | Licking time phase 1 (acute) and phase 2 (inflammatory) | Phase 1 | Phase 2 | Separates opioid from anti-inflammatory |
| Randall-Selitto | Pressure on inflamed paw | Threshold force producing withdrawal | Yes | Yes | Useful for anti-inflammatory analgesics |

---

## Anti-inflammatory models — comparison

| Model | Trigger | Paw volume by | Use |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Carrageenan paw oedema | Carrageenan 1% (sub-plantar) | Plethysmometer | Acute; prostaglandin-dependent |
| Adjuvant arthritis (Freund's) | Complete Freund's adjuvant | Plethysmometer + X-ray | Chronic; immune-mediated |
| Cotton pellet granuloma | Implanted pellets | Weight (dry) | Chronic; anti-fibrotic |
| Croton-oil ear oedema | Topical croton oil | Micrometer; ear punch weight | Topical anti-inflammatory |

**All models**: measure drug vs vehicle; express as % inhibition of inflammation.

---

## Toxicity study types

| Type | Duration | Animals | What it determines |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Acute toxicity | Single dose, 14-day observation | Rodents (rat, mouse) | LD₅₀; dose for sub-acute studies; clinical signs of toxicity |
| Sub-acute (28-day) | 28 days daily dosing | Rodents | Organ toxicity; reversibility |
| Sub-chronic (90-day) | 90 days | Rodents + non-rodent | NOAEL; regulatory requirement |
| Chronic | 6–24 months | Rodents + non-rodent | Carcinogenicity, cumulative toxicity |
| Reproductive | Females during gestation | Rat, rabbit | Teratogenicity, foetal toxicity |
| Genetic (Ames test) | — | *Salmonella* bacteria | Mutagenicity |

---

## Important calculations

| Formula | Symbol | Use |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Therapeutic index | TI = LD₅₀ / ED₅₀ | Safety measure; higher = safer |
| Protective index | PI = TD₅₀ / ED₅₀ | For neuropharmacology (TD = toxic dose) |
| Potency ratio (bioassay) | M = log T − log S (matched responses) | How many times more/less potent than standard |
| % inhibition (anti-inflammatory) | (control − treated) ÷ control × 100 | Efficacy of anti-inflammatory |
| Clearance | CL = dose / AUC | Rate of elimination per unit concentration |
| Volume of distribution | Vd = dose / C₀ | Apparent space for drug distribution |
| Half-life | t½ = 0.693 × Vd / CL | Time for concentration to halve |

---

## Exam reminder

- Section A (20 marks): expect one MCQ per model (hot plate / EPM / carrageenan / LD₅₀ / Schultz-Dale). Know the endpoint of each.
- Section B (10 marks each, 2 of 3): matched-dose bioassay method with calculation is a near-certain 10-mark question. Write the formula, the steps, and add a diagram of the organ bath setup.
- Section C (5 marks each, 7 of 9): one-preparation descriptions (Schultz-Dale sensitisation; tail-flick procedure; Ames test; organ bath mounting technique) all score well with a labelled diagram.
- For every in-vivo model: state animal species, route of administration, dose, endpoint measured, and what positive control is used.
- For every in-vitro preparation: state organ, species, bath solution, temperature, gas mixture (O₂/CO₂ or O₂), and contraction direction.

mcqs.explanation: Insulin is a heterogeneous polypeptide hormone; chemical assay cannot measure its biological activity directly. A bioassay using blood glucose in rabbits or the rat adipose tissue assay is used to assign potency in International Units.
mcqs.question: A bioassay is preferred over a chemical assay for which of the following substances?

mcqs.explanation: Quantal assays use an all-or-none response; at each dose, the fraction of animals responding is recorded. The ED50 or LD50 is estimated from this proportion vs log-dose relationship.
options: The proportion of animals showing a defined effect
The magnitude of the response in mm
The slope of the log-dose response line
The EC50 from the Emax model
mcqs.question: In a quantal bioassay, the endpoint is:

mcqs.explanation: EC50 is the concentration of drug producing half the maximum response (Emax). It is a measure of drug potency; a lower EC50 means greater potency.
options: The slope of the log-dose response curve
The concentration at which the Hill coefficient equals 1
mcqs.question: In the Emax model, the EC50 is:

mcqs.explanation: When n > 1 the dose-response curve is steeper than a simple hyperbola, indicating that binding at one site facilitates binding at subsequent sites (positive cooperativity), as seen with allosteric receptors.
mcqs.question: In the Hill equation, a Hill coefficient (n) greater than 1 indicates:

mcqs.explanation: λ = s / b. A lower λ means a more precise assay (less residual variability relative to the information provided by the slope). λ < 0.1 is excellent.
options: s / b, where s is residual SD and b is slope
b / s, where b is slope and s is residual SD
mcqs.question: The index of precision (λ) in a bioassay is defined as:

mcqs.explanation: Probit = 5 + z-score. At 50% response, z = 0, so probit = 5. This is the basis for reading the ED50 or LD50 from the probit-log dose line at probit 5.
mcqs.question: In probit analysis, probit 5 corresponds to:

mcqs.explanation: Parallelism is the key validity criterion: if the log-dose response lines of the standard and unknown are not parallel, the potency ratio varies with dose and cannot be expressed as a single number. The assay must be redesigned.
options: The two lines are not parallel
mcqs.question: The four-point parallel-line assay is invalid if:

mcqs.explanation: The LAL test is a full Replacement of the in-vivo rabbit pyrogen test using a cell-free in-vitro method. The other options are Reduction (crossover design) or Refinement (anaesthesia, humane endpoints).
options: Using the Limulus amoebocyte lysate test instead of the rabbit pyrogen test
Using a crossover design to reduce group size
Applying local anaesthesia before tail vein sampling
Using humane endpoints instead of death as an endpoint
mcqs.question: Which of the following is an example of Replacement under the 3Rs principle?

mcqs.explanation: CPCSEA is constituted under Section 15 of the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals Act, 1960. Its mandate is to regulate and supervise animal experiments in India.
options: Prevention of Cruelty to Animals Act, 1960
mcqs.question: CPCSEA in India operates under which legislation?

mcqs.explanation: The Latin square design is a balanced crossover in which each treatment appears once in each row (animal) and each column (period), so both sources of between-subject and between-period variability are removed from the residual error, increasing precision.
options: Remove both animal-to-animal and period-to-period variation from the error term
Increase the slope of the log-dose response line
mcqs.question: In a Latin square experimental design, the main purpose is to:

mcqs.explanation: Lorke's staged method uses 9 mice in Stage 1 (3 groups × 3) and 4 in Stage 2 (1 mouse × 4 doses) = 13 animals total, compared with the classical 50-animal method. It is a 3Rs-compliant approach.
mcqs.question: Which method uses only 13 mice to estimate the LD50?

mcqs.explanation: The up-and-down method is an economical sequential design in which only 5–10 animals may be needed; each animal's result determines the next dose. It sacrifices precision for economy.
options: The number of animals is very limited
Many doses are needed for probit analysis
A very precise LD50 with narrow confidence limits is needed
The dose-response curve is very steep
mcqs.question: The Dixon and Mood (up-and-down) method for LD50 estimation is best suited when:

mcqs.explanation: One IU of insulin equals 41.67 μg of the WHO 1st International Reference Preparation; the unit is arbitrary and historically defined in a rabbit blood glucose bioassay.
options: The hypoglycaemic potency of a specified mass (41.67 μg) of a reference preparation
The amount in 1 mL of a 1% solution
The amount that lowers blood glucose by 1 mmol/L in a human
The amount that contracts a guinea pig uterus by 1 mm
mcqs.question: A WHO International Standard for insulin defines 1 International Unit as:

mcqs.explanation: In a graded assay the actual degree of response is quantified, allowing a log-dose vs response regression line. This makes it more statistically efficient than a quantal assay.
options: The magnitude of response is measured on a continuous scale
The response is measured in a binary yes/no fashion
mcqs.question: Which of the following best describes a graded bioassay?

mcqs.explanation: Blinding prevents the observer from knowing which treatment an animal received, eliminating unconscious scoring bias. It is particularly important in subjective endpoints like behavioural tests.
mcqs.question: Blinding in animal experiments primarily removes:

mcqs.explanation: M = (mean response of unknown − mean response of standard) / b, where b is the common slope. The potency ratio R = antilog(M).
options: (Mean response of unknown − mean response of standard) / common slope
Slope × (mean response of unknown / mean response of standard)
Common slope / (mean response of unknown − mean response of standard)
mcqs.question: In a four-point parallel-line assay, the log-potency ratio M is calculated as:

mcqs.explanation: Humane endpoints are signs of severe distress (e.g., > 20% weight loss, laboured breathing) that trigger termination of the experiment before death, in line with the Refinement principle of the 3Rs.
options: A pre-specified criterion for early termination when an animal shows severe suffering
The dose that kills 50% of animals
The minimum number of animals per group
The washout period between doses in a crossover design
mcqs.question: A humane endpoint in an animal experiment is defined as:

mcqs.explanation: The sigmoidal log-dose response curve is approximately linear between 20% and 80% of Emax. Outside this range, the curve curves towards the baseline or the maximum, reducing the precision of interpolation.
mcqs.question: The linear region of the log-dose vs response curve, used for bioassay calculations, corresponds to responses between approximately:

mcqs.explanation: Heparin is a heterogeneous polysaccharide mixture; chemical assay measures carbohydrate content but cannot predict anticoagulant activity. The bioassay (clotting time test) assigns activity in International Units per batch.
options: It measures the actual anticoagulant activity, not just the amount of polymer present
It does not require a reference standard
It can be performed in cell-free systems
mcqs.question: Which advantage of bioassay over physicochemical assay is most important for a polypeptide drug like heparin?

mcqs.explanation: CPCSEA requires at least 7 members: veterinarian, animal care scientist, biological scientist, scientist using animals, institutional nominee, and 2 CPCSEA nominees (one must represent animal welfare outside the institution).
mcqs.question: The minimum number of members in an IAEC as required by CPCSEA is:

mcqs.explanation: The ionic composition, osmolality (~290 mOsm) and pH (7.4 when gassed with carbogen) of Krebs-Henseleit solution closely mimic interstitial fluid, allowing isolated tissues to maintain their function.
mcqs.question: The composition of Krebs-Henseleit solution is designed to mimic which body fluid?

mcqs.explanation: Carbogen (95% O2 / 5% CO2) both oxygenates the tissue and maintains the bicarbonate buffer at pH 7.4. Pure O2 would drive off CO2 and raise pH, disrupting the buffer.
mcqs.question: The gas mixture used to oxygenate an isolated mammalian tissue bath is typically:

mcqs.explanation: The guinea pig ileum has abundant H1 receptors in the longitudinal smooth muscle and responds to histamine at concentrations as low as 1 ng/mL, making it the most sensitive standard preparation for histamine bioassay.
mcqs.question: Which isolated preparation is most sensitive for bioassay of histamine?

mcqs.explanation: The frog rectus abdominis has nicotinic (N-M type) receptors. Atropine (muscarinic antagonist) does not block the ACh contraction; tubocurarine (nicotinic antagonist) does. This confirms that the bioassay measures nicotinic activity.
options: It has nicotinic receptors and atropine does not block the response
It responds to histamine and ACh equally
mcqs.question: The frog rectus abdominis preparation is used for bioassay of acetylcholine because:

mcqs.explanation: The oestrogen-primed rat uterus is the official WHO preparation for oxytocin standardisation. Oestrogen upregulates oxytocin receptors, maximising sensitivity to the hormone.
mcqs.question: Which preparation is used as the official WHO preparation for standardising oxytocin?

mcqs.explanation: The Schild equation log(r−1) = log[B] − pA2 predicts a slope of 1 for competitive (orthosteric), reversible antagonism. A slope significantly different from 1 indicates non-competitive binding or allosteric interaction.
mcqs.question: In the Schild plot, a slope of exactly 1 indicates:

mcqs.explanation: pA2 = -log[B], where [B] is the antagonist concentration that requires a 2-fold increase in agonist concentration to restore the original response (dose ratio = 2). Higher pA2 means higher potency.
options: The negative log of the molar concentration that doubles the agonist EC50
The molar concentration causing 50% inhibition of the agonist maximum response
The slope of the log-dose response line
mcqs.question: The pA2 of an antagonist is defined as:

mcqs.explanation: Antigen-antibody reaction on mast cells in the gut wall causes degranulation and release of histamine. Mepyramine (H1 antagonist) blocks the response, confirming H1 mediation.
options: Histamine released from mast cells acting on H1 receptors
Acetylcholine released from intrinsic nerve endings
mcqs.question: In the Schultz-Dale reaction, the contraction of the sensitised guinea pig ileum in response to antigen is primarily mediated by:

mcqs.explanation: A preload of 0.5–1 g tension is applied to put the longitudinal smooth muscle under slight stretch, which maintains sensitivity to agonists and reduces spontaneous tone variation.
mcqs.question: What is the resting tension (preload) typically applied to a guinea pig ileum preparation?

mcqs.explanation: The double-walled (jacketed) design allows thermostated water to circulate in the outer jacket, maintaining the inner bath and its contents at a precise, constant temperature — usually 37°C for mammalian tissues.
options: Increase the volume of Krebs solution
Provide electrical isolation for the transducer
Maintain the bath at a constant temperature via circulating warm water
Act as a reservoir for drug additions
mcqs.question: In the organ bath, the purpose of the jacketed outer chamber is to:

mcqs.explanation: α1-adrenoceptor activation by noradrenaline or phenylephrine increases the frequency and amplitude of spontaneous contractions. β2-adrenoceptor stimulation (adrenaline at low doses) relaxes the preparation.
mcqs.question: The rabbit duodenum preparation shows spontaneous contractions that are increased by:

mcqs.explanation: Glucose (11 mmol/L) is the energy substrate for oxidative phosphorylation in the isolated tissue. Depletion of glucose leads to rapid loss of contractility.
mcqs.question: Which component of the Krebs-Henseleit solution functions as the metabolic substrate for the isolated tissue?

mcqs.explanation: The classic three-point assay cycle is S1 (low standard) → U (unknown) → S2 (high standard), with complete washout between each dose. The unknown response is interpolated on the S1-S2 log-dose line.
mcqs.question: In the three-point assay for ACh on frog rectus, the dose cycle used is:

mcqs.explanation: Oestrogen increases the density of oxytocin receptors in uterine smooth muscle, making the preparation highly sensitive to oxytocin. Without priming the uterus shows a minimal, inconsistent response.
options: Oestrogen directly contracts uterine smooth muscle
Oestrogen increases calcium in the bath
mcqs.question: Oestrogen priming of the rat uterus for oxytocin bioassay is essential because:

mcqs.explanation: An isometric transducer measures force (tension) at constant length. This is preferred because the results are more reproducible than isotonic (constant load, variable length) recordings, as muscle properties change with length.
options: Muscle shortening at a constant load
Temperature changes in the organ bath
Change in muscle tension while muscle length is kept constant
mcqs.question: An isometric force transducer measures:

mcqs.explanation: Calcium ions (CaCl2 2.5 mmol/L) provide the extracellular calcium source for activation of the contractile machinery via calmodulin-dependent myosin light chain kinase in smooth muscle.
mcqs.question: Which ionic component of Krebs solution is essential for excitation-contraction coupling in smooth muscle?

mcqs.explanation: De Jalon solution has a lower calcium concentration than Krebs solution. This reduces spontaneous myogenic activity of the uterus, allowing cleaner contractile responses to oxytocin.
mcqs.question: What de Jalon solution differs from Krebs-Henseleit in that it has:

mcqs.explanation: During equilibration, the tissue releases metabolic products (CO2, lactic acid) and any residual endogenous mediators. Washing removes these and ensures the tissue starts each dose in a standard environment.
options: Increase the temperature of the bath
Remove accumulated metabolic waste products and maintain a fresh ionic environment
mcqs.question: During the equilibration period of an organ bath preparation, the purpose of periodic washing with fresh Krebs solution is to:

mcqs.explanation: Both parallelism and linearity must be satisfied. Significant non-linearity means the assumed log-linear model does not describe the data correctly, so the potency estimate from the slope is unreliable.
options: Invalid only if the quadratic terms differ between lines
Invalid because the linearity validity criterion is not met
mcqs.question: In a four-point assay, if the two log-dose response lines are parallel but neither is linear (both show significant quadratic deviation), the assay is:

mcqs.explanation: The guinea pig ileum from an actively sensitised animal contains abundant mast cells bearing IgE specific for the sensitising antigen. Antigen challenge triggers mast cell degranulation and histamine release, contracting the longitudinal smooth muscle.
options: Guinea pig ileum from a sensitised animal
mcqs.question: Which preparation is most appropriate for demonstrating the Schultz-Dale reaction for anaphylaxis?

mcqs.explanation: The rat gastric fundus strip has abundant 5-HT2 receptors and is relatively insensitive to histamine, making it the preferred preparation for 5-HT bioassay. Ketanserin or methysergide confirms 5-HT2 mediation.
mcqs.question: The rat fundus strip is most selective for bioassay of:

mcqs.explanation: Angiotensin I requires ACE-mediated conversion to angiotensin II to exert its full pressor effect. Captopril (ACE inhibitor) blocks this conversion; the residual pressor effect of Ang I is abolished. Ang II is unaffected.
options: Captopril inhibits ACE, preventing conversion of angiotensin I to angiotensin II
mcqs.question: The pressor response to angiotensin I is abolished by captopril because:

mcqs.explanation: In an anaesthetised cat, ACh produces a fall in BP (muscarinic). After atropine blocks the muscarinic component, the same dose of ACh now shows a rise in BP — the nicotinic component (ganglionic stimulation releasing catecholamines) unmasked.
options: The fall in blood pressure after adrenaline in an alpha-blocked cat
The paradoxical fall in blood pressure after noradrenaline
The unmasking of a rise in blood pressure after ACh injection following atropine
The reversal of bradycardia by atropine
mcqs.question: Dale's vasomotor reversal refers to:

mcqs.explanation: In cascade superfusion the perfusate flows over each selective tissue in turn; all receive the same concentration. Combined with selective blockers on individual tissues, multiple autacoids in one sample can be identified simultaneously.
options: Each preparation receives the same concentration of test substance simultaneously, allowing simultaneous identification of multiple autacoids
The preparation sequence amplifies the drug concentration
The tissues are exposed to different temperatures
It eliminates the need for Krebs solution
mcqs.question: In cascade superfusion, what is the advantage of using multiple tissue preparations in series?

mcqs.explanation: Phase 2 oedema (1–3 h post-carrageenan) is driven by prostaglandins (PGE2, PGI2) produced via inducible COX-2. NSAIDs are most active at this phase, which is why the 3-hour time point is used for NSAID screening.
mcqs.question: Which autacoid is primarily responsible for the Phase 2 (1–3 h) oedema in the carrageenan paw oedema model?

mcqs.explanation: Bradykinin acts on B2 (bradykinin) receptors expressed on the smooth muscle and intrinsic neurons of the guinea pig ileum. The contraction is slower and more sustained than the histamine response.
mcqs.question: Bradykinin contracts the guinea pig ileum through:

mcqs.explanation: ACh slows the frog heart through muscarinic M2 receptors (Gi, reduced cAMP, reduced If and ICa,L currents). This is the basis of the cardio-inhibitory bioassay; atropine abolishes the response.
options: Nicotinic receptors at the neuromuscular junction
Muscarinic M2 receptors reducing rate and force
mcqs.question: The bioassay of ACh on the isolated frog heart exploits its effect on:

mcqs.explanation: Mepyramine (pyrilamine) is a selective, competitive H1 receptor antagonist. If the contraction is blocked by mepyramine but not by atropine or methysergide, it is confirmed as an H1-mediated histamine response.
mcqs.question: Which antagonist is used to confirm that a contraction of the guinea pig ileum is mediated by H1 receptors?

questions.answer:
1. Definition: a bioassay (biological assay) is a procedure that uses a living organism or its components to estimate the potency or concentration of a substance by comparing its effect with that of a reference standard of known potency.
2. Need for bioassay: used when the substance is chemically undefined, structurally heterogeneous (e.g., insulin, heparin, digitalis) or when biological activity cannot be predicted from chemical content alone.
3. Advantages: measures actual biological activity; detects pharmacologically active impurities; applicable to heterogeneous mixtures; identifies unknown contaminants invisible to chemical analysis.
4. Limitations: biological variability is higher than chemical methods; requires living systems under strict conditions; influenced by species, age, sex and strain; more time-consuming and expensive; subject to ethical constraints.
5. Classification by nature of response: (a) Quantal (all-or-none): the response is binary — it either occurs or does not. Examples: death or survival, sleeping time, convulsion. The endpoint is the proportion responding at each dose, from which ED50 or LD50 is calculated by probit analysis. Each animal gives only one observation. (b) Graded: the response is measured on a continuous scale — height of contraction, change in blood pressure in mmHg, change in heart rate. Each animal or tissue can receive multiple doses. The degree of response is recorded against dose, and potency is estimated from relative positions of log-dose response lines.
6. Comparison table: quantal assay gives proportion responding vs dose; uses ED50/LD50; large group sizes needed. Graded assay gives magnitude vs dose; uses slope, Emax, EC50; more efficient per animal.
7. Dose-response relationships: at low doses the response increases with dose; at high doses it plateaus as receptors become saturated.
8. The Emax model: Effect = Emax × [D] / (EC50 + [D]). Emax is the maximum achievable effect; EC50 is the concentration producing 50% of Emax. This describes simple competitive receptor occupancy (Langmuir isotherm). On a log-dose axis the relationship is sigmoidal.
9. Hill equation (sigmoidal Emax): Effect = Emax × [D]^n / (EC50^n + [D]^n), where n is the Hill coefficient. When n = 1 the equation reduces to the Emax model. When n > 1 the curve is steeper (cooperativity); n < 1 gives a shallower curve. The Hill equation fits allosteric and ion-channel-linked receptors.
10. Log-dose vs response: plotting log(dose) on the x-axis converts the hyperbolic curve to a sigmoid; the region from 20% to 80% of Emax is approximately linear and is used for bioassay calculations and for constructing standard curves.

questions.answer:
1. Principle: two doses each of the standard (S1, S2) and the unknown preparation (U1, U2) are used. The dose ratio S1:S2 is kept equal to U1:U2 (typically 1:3 or 1:4). Both log-dose response lines must be parallel and linear for the assay to be valid.
2. The horizontal distance between the two parallel lines on the log-dose axis is the log-potency ratio (M).
3. Procedure: (a) Prepare two doses of standard and two doses of unknown with the same dose ratio. (b) Record responses for all four doses (multiple replicates — usually 4–6 observations per dose). (c) Plot log-dose vs response and fit linear regression lines to each set.
4. Calculation of log-potency ratio M: M = (mean response of unknown - mean response of standard) / b, where b is the common slope of the two lines (derived from the pooled regression). Potency ratio R = antilog(M). Potency of unknown = R × (labelled potency of standard per unit dose).
5. Worked example: if S1 = 10 units → 18 mm, S2 = 30 units → 30 mm, U1 → 24 mm, U2 → 36 mm; b = 12/0.477 = 25.16; mean response standard = 24, mean response unknown = 30; M = (30 - 24)/25.16 = 0.238; R = antilog(0.238) = 1.73. Unknown true potency = 1.73 × labelled dose of standard.
6. Validity tests (from ANOVA): (a) Regression — the slope b must be significantly non-zero; a flat line contains no information. (b) Parallelism — the difference in slopes of the two lines must not be statistically significant; if the lines are not parallel the potency ratio is not constant across doses, invalidating the assay. (c) Linearity — neither line must show significant non-linearity (quadratic deviation). (d) Preparations — the difference in blank responses of standard and unknown preparations must not be significant.
7. If validity tests fail: a failed parallelism test means the two preparations are not pharmacologically equivalent at the receptor (the unknown may contain additional active or inhibitory substances). The assay must be redesigned.
8. Index of precision λ: λ = s / b, where s is the residual standard deviation of responses about the fitted lines, and b is the common slope. A lower λ indicates a more precise assay. λ < 0.1 is excellent; λ > 0.2 is poor. Precision improves by reducing variability (more stable tissue, better technique) and increasing the slope (steeper dose-response relationship, e.g. by selecting a more sensitive tissue).
9. Fiducial limits of the potency estimate: the 95% fiducial limits (confidence limits) of M are M ± 1.96 × s_M, where s_M is the standard error of the log-potency estimate. The potency limits are antilog(M ± 1.96 × s_M). Narrower limits mean a more reliable assay.
10. Applications: standard method for bioassay of insulin (on blood glucose in rabbits), oxytocin (on rat uterus), heparin (on clotting time), digitalis (on frog heart), and many vaccines and hormones for WHO international standardisation.

questions.answer:
1. Historical context: the use of animals in pharmacological research has always required ethical justification. The seminal work of Russell and Burch (1959) formalised the ethical framework as the 3Rs.
2. Replacement: finding methods that avoid or replace the use of animals entirely or partially. Full replacement includes cell-based assays (human primary cells, cell lines), computer modelling, organ-on-a-chip, in-silico pharmacokinetic models, and physicochemical tests. Partial replacement substitutes lower organisms (Drosophila, Caenorhabditis elegans, zebrafish larvae) for mammals. Example: the Limulus amoebocyte lysate (LAL) test replaced the rabbit pyrogen test; human cell-based bioassays replaced animal bioassays for many cytokines and growth factors.
3. Reduction: using the minimum number of animals needed to answer the scientific question reliably. Strategies include: proper statistical power calculations to determine group sizes; using crossover designs (each animal is its own control, so fewer animals are needed); sharing tissues between experiments; using pilot data to narrow dose ranges before the full study; systematic review to avoid replicating work already done.
4. Refinement: modifying procedures to minimise pain, distress and suffering in animals that must still be used. Examples include: using local anaesthesia or appropriate systemic analgesia; selecting minimally invasive routes of administration; training animals to cooperate with the procedure (reducing stress); providing environmental enrichment (nesting material, social housing); using humane endpoints.
5. Humane endpoints: pre-specified criteria for early termination of a study when an animal shows severe suffering, without waiting for death. Examples: weight loss exceeding 20%, laboured or dyspnoeic breathing, inability to reach food or water, persistent prostration, severe skin lesions. Using humane endpoints is both more ethical and more scientifically valid than using death as an endpoint, because a moribund animal's data are unreliable.
6. CPCSEA: the Committee for the Purpose of Control and Supervision of Experiments on Animals operates under the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals Act, 1960, in India. Every institution that uses animals for scientific purposes must register with CPCSEA.
7. IAEC composition: an Institutional Animal Ethics Committee must include: a veterinarian responsible for the facility; a scientist in charge of animal care; a biological scientist; a scientist from a different biological discipline who uses animals; a nominee of the institutional head; and two nominees from CPCSEA, one of whom must represent animal welfare interests outside the institution.
8. IAEC role: reviews and approves all protocols before work begins; monitors ongoing experiments; ensures compliance with CPCSEA standards for housing, feeding, anaesthesia and anaesthetic monitoring; inspects the animal facility periodically.
9. Randomisation: assigns animals to treatment groups by a random process (random number tables, computer-generated sequences), eliminating systematic bias in group allocation. Without randomisation, factors such as cage position, litter origin or body weight might be unevenly distributed between groups, confounding the results.
10. Blinding: single blinding — the person handling and dosing the animals does not know which animal received which treatment. Double blinding — both the dosing person and the person measuring or scoring outcomes are blinded. Blinding removes unconscious measurement bias (the observer expecting a drug to work may unconsciously score ambiguous responses as positive). Double blinding is especially important in behavioural endpoints like the elevated plus maze or forced swim test.
11. Study design: parallel design — each animal receives one treatment only; more animals are needed but carry-over effects are avoided. Crossover design — each animal receives all treatments sequentially with washout periods; fewer animals needed but requires stable preparation. Latin square design — balances both animal-to-animal and period-to-period variation; used when multiple treatments and periods are needed.

questions.answer:
Definition: a bioassay is a procedure that uses a living organism or its components to measure the potency of a substance by comparing its biological effect with that of a reference standard.
Quantal bioassay: the response is binary — it either occurs or it does not. The endpoint is the proportion of subjects showing the response at each dose. Examples: LD50 determination (death or survival), sleeping time test (sleep or no sleep), convulsion threshold. Statistical analysis: probit analysis gives ED50 or LD50. Each subject contributes one yes/no data point, so larger groups are needed.
Graded bioassay: the response is measured on a continuous numerical scale — height of contraction in mm, blood pressure change in mmHg, heart rate change. Examples: frog rectus abdominis (acetylcholine contraction height), guinea pig ileum (histamine contraction), blood pressure in an anaesthetised rat. Each animal or tissue gives multiple observations at different doses, making graded assays more efficient per animal.
Key distinction: quantal assays deal with probability (proportion responding); graded assays deal with magnitude. Graded assays allow construction of a linear log-dose response line and direct calculation of potency ratio, index of precision and fiducial limits from the same experiment.

The 3Rs framework was established by Russell and Burch (1959) as the ethical basis for animal experimentation.
Replacement: finding methods that avoid or replace the use of animals. Full replacement substitutes in-vitro cell-based assays, computer models, organ-on-a-chip systems, Limulus amoebocyte lysate (LAL) test for pyrogens (replaced the rabbit pyrogen test), or physicochemical methods. Partial replacement uses lower organisms such as Drosophila or zebrafish instead of mammals, since they have fewer welfare protections.
Reduction: using the fewest animals necessary to obtain reliable data. Strategies: power calculations to determine the minimum group size, crossover designs where each animal is its own control, in-vitro screening to narrow doses before in-vivo testing, sharing tissues from one animal between multiple experiments, and systematic literature review to avoid repeating existing work.
Refinement: modifying procedures so that surviving animals experience the least possible pain, distress or suffering. Examples: appropriate anaesthesia and analgesia during surgical procedures, the use of humane endpoints (stopping an experiment when the animal shows specified distress criteria rather than waiting for death), environmental enrichment (providing nesting material, social housing), training animals to cooperate with procedures, and using minimally invasive blood collection techniques.
In India CPCSEA enforces the 3Rs through mandatory IAEC review of all protocols.

questions.answer:
Probit analysis converts the cumulative frequency distribution of a quantal dose-response relationship from a sigmoidal curve to a straight line, enabling precise estimation of the LD50.
Probit transformation: a probit is defined as 5 plus the z-score corresponding to the proportion responding. Probit 5 corresponds to the 50% response (z = 0); probit 6 to 84.1% (z = +1); probit 4 to 15.9% (z = -1). By definition, the LD50 is the dose at which the probit = 5.
Procedure: (1) Administer test substance at four to six doses spanning the expected LD50 range; use at least 10 animals per group. (2) Record the proportion dying at each dose and calculate probit values. (3) Plot probit vs log-dose; fit a straight line by weighted least squares (the weight of each point is the product of the group size and the weighting coefficient from probit tables). (4) Read the log-dose corresponding to probit 5 — this is the log-LD50. (5) The antilog of this value is the LD50.
Fiducial limits: the 95% confidence interval of the LD50 is computed from the variance of the fitted line; narrower limits indicate a more precise estimate.
Comparison with other methods: the moving averages method and Dixon-Mood up-and-down method are simpler but give less information; probit analysis gives full confidence limits, the slope (which characterises the dose-response steepness), and allows formal validity testing. For regulatory submissions probit analysis is the preferred method.

CPCSEA (Committee for the Purpose of Control and Supervision of Experiments on Animals) was established under the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals Act, 1960, in India. It is the apex regulatory body for animal experimentation.
Key requirements: (1) Every institution performing animal experiments must register with CPCSEA. Registration requires adequate animal facility with prescribed standards of housing, nutrition, environmental enrichment and veterinary care. (2) An Institutional Animal Ethics Committee (IAEC) must be constituted and must approve every animal experiment protocol before work begins. (3) Animals must be housed in species-appropriate cages with adequate space, bedding, temperature (22±2°C), humidity (45–65%), 12:12 light-dark cycle, and social housing where species requirements allow. (4) All surgical procedures must use appropriate anaesthesia; animals must be monitored until recovery. (5) Humane endpoints must be specified in every protocol.
IAEC composition (minimum 7 members): (a) a veterinarian affiliated to the institution, responsible for animal care; (b) the scientist in charge of the animal house or facility; (c) a biological scientist with experience in animal experimentation; (d) a scientist from a biological discipline who uses animals but is not from the applicant's department; (e) a nominee of the head of the institution; (f) a nominee from CPCSEA, who is a scientist; (g) a second nominee from CPCSEA who represents animal welfare and is not a scientist from within the institution.
The IAEC reviews the 3Rs application, the number of animals justified, the suitability of anaesthesia, and the provisions for humane endpoints in each protocol submitted.

questions.answer:
Index of precision (λ): defined as λ = s / b, where s is the standard deviation of observations about the fitted log-dose response line (the residual standard deviation), and b is the slope of the line in units of response per log-dose unit.
Interpretation: λ reflects how much of the total variability in response is accounted for by the dose-response relationship, relative to the unaccounted residual variability. A lower λ means more of the variation is due to dose, and the response per unit change in log-dose is large relative to noise. λ < 0.1 is considered excellent; 0.1–0.2 is acceptable; > 0.2 is poor and may require redesign.
How to improve λ: reduce biological variability (use a more uniform animal strain, carefully control temperature and oxygenation); increase the slope b (choose a more sensitive preparation or a narrower dose range on the steepest part of the curve); increase replication at each dose point.
Fiducial limits (confidence limits) of the potency estimate: the 95% fiducial limits of the log-potency ratio M are M ± 1.96 × standard error of M. The potency limits are expressed as antilog(M ± 1.96 × s_M), giving a range within which the true potency lies with 95% probability.
Use in quality control: if the 95% fiducial limits of a batch of biological medicine are within the pharmacopoeial allowed range (e.g., 80–125%), the batch passes the potency test. The index of precision determines the precision of the determination; the fiducial limits define the allowable uncertainty. An assay with a large λ gives wide fiducial limits, which may fail to meet the pharmacopoeial acceptance criterion.

questions.answer:
1. Principle: an isolated tissue removed from the body retains pharmacological responsiveness for one to several hours when maintained in a nutrient solution at the correct temperature with continuous oxygenation.
2. Components of the organ bath: (a) glass or polycarbonate inner bath containing the tissue and Krebs solution; (b) a jacketed outer chamber through which thermostated water is circulated to maintain a constant temperature (37°C for mammalian tissues, 25°C for amphibian); (c) a gas inlet tube for constant bubbling of carbogen (95% O2 / 5% CO2) or pure O2; (d) two hooks for mounting the tissue — the lower hook is fixed to the bath bottom, the upper hook is connected by a thread to the transducer; (e) a drain tap for rapid washout; (f) an isometric force transducer (strain gauge) connected to an amplifier and recorder.
3. Types: simple organ bath (glass cylinder immersed in a water bath) for routine work; Trendelenburg bath with an angled or U-shaped design for intestinal preparations; jacketed organ bath (double-walled) for precise temperature control.
4. Krebs-Henseleit solution composition: NaCl 118 mmol/L, KCl 4.7, CaCl2 2.5, MgSO4 1.2, KH2PO4 1.2, NaHCO3 25, glucose 11. The bicarbonate buffer with CO2 maintains pH 7.4. Calcium provides excitation-contraction coupling. Glucose is the metabolic substrate. The osmolality (approximately 290 mOsm) matches interstitial fluid.
5. Oxygenation: carbogen provides oxygen and removes CO2; the bicarbonate/CO2 pair forms the buffer. Without oxygenation, tissues lose contractility within minutes due to ATP depletion.
6. Equilibration period: 30–60 minutes of washing with fresh Krebs at 37°C before the bioassay begins. During equilibration, the tissue recovers from mechanical handling and reaches a stable resting tension (preload).
7. Isolated tissue preparations table:
(a) Frog rectus abdominis — frog — nicotinic ACh receptors (N-M type) — contraction — bioassay of ACh and nicotinic agonists; study of neuromuscular blockers.
(b) Guinea pig ileum — guinea pig — H1 (histamine), B2 (bradykinin), 5-HT3, μ-opioid, muscarinic — contraction — most versatile preparation; Schultz-Dale anaphylaxis reaction.
(c) Rabbit duodenum — rabbit — α1-adrenoceptor (contraction), β2-adrenoceptor (relaxation) — spontaneous contractions increase/decrease — bioassay of catecholamines, adrenoceptor studies.
(d) Rabbit jejunum — rabbit — oxytocin receptor, prostaglandin receptors — contraction — bioassay of oxytocin and prostaglandins.
(e) Rat uterus (oestrogen-sensitised) — rat in oestrus — oxytocin, bradykinin, ergometrine — phasic contractions — WHO oxytocin standardisation; most sensitive preparation for oxytocin.
(f) Rat fundus strip — rat — 5-HT2 receptor, prostaglandins — contraction — selective 5-HT bioassay; NSAID effect on prostaglandins.
8. Mounting the tissue: cut the tissue to 2–3 cm; avoid crushing the ends used for hooks; mount with the longitudinal muscle axis vertical; apply a resting tension (0.5–1 g for guinea pig ileum, 0.5 g for rat uterus).
9. Transducers: isometric transducers measure tension at constant length; they are more reproducible than isotonic transducers and are universally used in modern pharmacology.
10. After the bioassay: cumulative dose-response curves are constructed by adding successive doses of agonist without washing between additions, allowing each concentration to equilibrate (3–5 min); alternatively, non-cumulative protocols wash after each dose and are preferred for bioassay calculations.

questions.answer:
1. Three-point assay principle: three doses are used in a cycle: low standard (S1), unknown (U), high standard (S2). The cycle is repeated at least 4–6 times. The mean responses for S1, U and S2 are averaged across all cycles. The response of the unknown is interpolated on the log-dose response line drawn between S1 and S2.
2. Frog rectus preparation: the rectus abdominis muscle from a frog is mounted in frog Ringer's solution at 25°C. Acetylcholine contracts it by activating nicotinic receptors. Atropine does not block the response; tubocurarine does. Sensitivity: 1–100 ng/mL.
3. Procedure: mount the muscle, equilibrate 30 min, verify viability with ACh. Run cycles SUSUS (S1, U, S2 alternate with S1 at the start of each cycle) with 1–2 min between doses and complete washout between doses.
4. Worked calculation:
   S1 = 10 ng ACh → mean contraction 15 mm
   S2 = 40 ng ACh → mean contraction 32 mm
   U = 0.1 mL of unknown → mean contraction 22 mm
   Linear log-dose line from S1 to S2:
     Slope b = (32 - 15) / (log40 - log10) = 17 / (1.602 - 1.000) = 17 / 0.602 = 28.24 mm per log unit
   Log-dose of ACh equivalent to U:
     log(dose_U) = 1.000 + (22 - 15) / 28.24 = 1.000 + 0.248 = 1.248
     Dose equivalent = antilog(1.248) = 17.7 ng ACh per bath
   Volume added = 0.1 mL, so concentration in unknown = 17.7 / 0.1 = 177 ng/mL
5. Validity: the response of the unknown must fall between those of S1 and S2 (bracketing). If U > S2 or U < S1, the dose of U must be adjusted for the next run.
6. pA2 and Schild plot principle: pA2 is the negative log of the molar concentration of a competitive antagonist that requires a doubling of the agonist dose to restore the original response. It is a quantitative measure of competitive antagonist potency.
7. Procedure: (a) Construct an agonist CRC without antagonist; note EC50 (= D). (b) Allow equilibration with antagonist concentration B1; repeat the agonist CRC; note new EC50 (D'). (c) Calculate dose ratio r = D' / D. (d) Repeat for at least three antagonist concentrations B1, B2, B3.
8. Schild equation: log(r - 1) = log(B) - pA2. This is a straight line with slope 1.0 and x-intercept = pA2.
9. Schild plot: plot log(r - 1) on the y-axis vs log(B) on the x-axis. If the antagonism is competitive and reversible the slope is 1.0 and the x-intercept gives pA2. A slope significantly different from 1 suggests non-competitive antagonism, irreversible binding or allosteric modulation.
10. Example: mepyramine (H1 antagonist) has a pA2 of approximately 9.0 on guinea pig ileum against histamine; this means 1 nmol/L mepyramine doubles the histamine EC50. Higher pA2 = more potent antagonist.

questions.answer:
1. The guinea pig ileum is the most sensitive preparation for histamine bioassay. It responds to histamine through H1 receptors in the longitudinal smooth muscle layer with a graded contraction measured in mm on a kymograph or recorder.
2. Preparation: sacrifice a guinea pig; remove a 2–3 cm segment of ileum; place in cold Krebs; mount between two hooks in a 25 mL jacketed organ bath; apply 1 g tension; equilibrate 45 min in Krebs at 37°C with carbogen (95% O2 / 5% CO2).
3. Confirm viability: add histamine 10 ng/mL; record contraction; wash thoroughly; repeat three times to ensure reproducible responses.
4. Dose selection: doses must be in the linear portion of the log-dose response curve (20–80% of maximum response). For the four-point assay choose two doses of standard histamine (e.g., 10 and 30 ng/mL, dose ratio 3) and two doses of unknown at the same dose ratio.
5. Assay sequence: alternate standard (S1, S2) and unknown (U1, U2) doses with complete washout (3 bath volumes of Krebs) between each dose and at least 3 min equilibration time. Run at least 4 replicates of each dose point.
6. Calculation: mean responses: S1 → ys1, S2 → ys2, U1 → yu1, U2 → yu2. Slope of standard line: bs = (ys2 - ys1) / (logS2 - logS1). Slope of unknown line: bu = (yu2 - yu1) / (logU1 ratio). Common slope b = (bs + bu) / 2 (or pooled regression). Log-potency ratio M = [(yu1 + yu2)/2 - (ys1 + ys2)/2] / b. Potency ratio R = antilog(M).
7. Validity tests from ANOVA: (a) regression — b must be statistically significant; (b) parallelism — bs and bu must not differ significantly; (c) linearity — no significant quadratic departure; (d) preparations — mean responses of standard and unknown must not differ significantly from zero.
8. Index of precision λ = s / b, where s is the residual SD from the within-treatment ANOVA. λ < 0.1 is excellent; > 0.2 requires redesign.
9. Fiducial limits: 95% fiducial limits of potency = antilog[M ± (1.96 × s × √(2 × sum of 1/n) / b)]. Narrow limits indicate a reliable assay.
10. Specificity: add mepyramine (H1 antagonist) to confirm that the response is H1-mediated. Add atropine to confirm that the muscarinic component (from intrinsic ACh release by distension) is separated. The bioassay is then selective for exogenous histamine.

Krebs-Henseleit solution composition (approximate mmol/L): NaCl 118; KCl 4.7; CaCl2 2.5; MgSO4 1.2; KH2PO4 1.2; NaHCO3 25; glucose 11.
Purposes of key components: NaCl and KCl maintain the ionic environment and membrane potential; CaCl2 provides calcium for excitation-contraction coupling; MgSO4 antagonises calcium where necessary; NaHCO3 is the buffer — with CO2 from the gas mixture it maintains pH 7.4 by the bicarbonate buffer system; glucose provides the energy substrate for the tissue; oxygenation with carbogen supplies O2 for oxidative phosphorylation and maintains pH through CO2/HCO3 equilibrium. The osmolality (~290 mOsm) matches mammalian interstitial fluid, preventing cell swelling or shrinkage.

Oestrogen priming: oxytocin receptors are upregulated by oestrogen in the uterine smooth muscle. Without oestrogen priming, the rat uterus has very few oxytocin receptors and shows a poor, inconsistent response. Oestrogen is administered as stilboestrol (5 μg/kg s.c.) 18–24 hours before the experiment (or the rat is killed during natural oestrus, confirmed by vaginal smear showing a predominantly cornified cell pattern).
Preparation: sacrifice the rat by cervical dislocation; remove one uterine horn; mount a 2–3 cm strip in De Jalon solution (a low-calcium modified Ringer; low calcium reduces spontaneous contractility and allows cleaner oxytocin responses) at 30°C; apply 0.5 g tension; oxygenate with air; equilibrate for 30–45 minutes.
Bioassay procedure: use the WHO 2nd International Standard for oxytocin (defined in milli-International Units per mL, mIU/mL). Construct a standard curve with 0.5, 1 and 2 mIU/mL. The response is the height of phasic contractions (mm). Test the unknown preparation at a volume in the same response range and read off the potency from the standard curve by interpolation.
Specificity: the response to oxytocin is blocked by atosiban (oxytocin/vasopressin antagonist). Ergometrine (sustained tonic contraction) is distinguished from oxytocin (phasic contractions). PGF2α also contracts the rat uterus, but the response is not blocked by atosiban.
Use: official WHO method for standardisation of oxytocin preparations for clinical use.

questions.answer:
Background: Type I (immediate) hypersensitivity reactions are mediated by IgE antibodies bound to mast cell surface Fc receptors. When an antigen bridges two adjacent IgE molecules, it triggers mast cell degranulation, releasing histamine, leukotrienes, prostaglandins and other mediators.
Schultz-Dale reaction procedure: an actively sensitised guinea pig is used (sensitised by injecting a small dose of antigen such as egg albumin 2–3 weeks previously, so that the animal has mounted an IgE response). The ileum is removed and mounted in an organ bath in the usual way. When a small amount of the specific antigen is added to the bath, the antigen contacts the IgE on mast cells in the wall of the gut. The antigen-antibody interaction triggers degranulation, and the released histamine (and other mediators) contracts the longitudinal smooth muscle. This contraction is the Schultz-Dale reaction.
Information provided: (1) confirms active sensitisation to the antigen; (2) the response is abolished by mepyramine (H1 antagonist), confirming histamine as the principal mediator; (3) indomethacin reduces a portion of the response, suggesting that prostaglandins also contribute; (4) the reaction can be used to test anti-allergic drugs — antihistamines, sodium cromoglycate (mast cell stabiliser) and corticosteroids each reduce the response by different mechanisms; (5) the in-vitro Schultz-Dale response closely mimics the in-vivo active anaphylaxis reaction, allowing its study without the welfare costs of systemic anaphylaxis.

questions.answer:
Matching bioassay: the dose of the unknown that produces the same response as a chosen dose of the standard is determined. The potency ratio is calculated directly: Potency = (Dose of standard producing the matched response) / (Dose of unknown producing the matched response) × stated potency of standard per unit dose. It requires only a single response level and is very rapid. Used for quick screening or when only a few data points are available. Limitation: assumes linearity at the matched response point, and the response level must be in the mid-range of the curve.
Bracketing (two-point) assay: two doses of the standard (S_low, S_high) bracket the response of the unknown (the unknown response falls between the two standard responses). Log-dose is interpolated: log(dose_U) = log(S_low) + [(r_U - r_low) / (r_high - r_low)] × [log(S_high) - log(S_low)]. Potency of unknown = antilog(log dose_U) / volume of unknown added × stated standard potency. Used when a rapid estimate is needed with two doses of standard; more reliable than matching because two data points define the linear range. No assumption about which part of the curve is linear — the two standards bracket the actual response.
Comparison: matching uses one dose of standard and one of unknown (minimum data); bracketing uses two doses of standard and one of unknown (more information, more reliable); the four-point parallel-line assay uses two doses each of standard and unknown with full ANOVA validity testing (most rigorous, pharmacopoeial standard).

questions.answer:
Principle: the rabbit duodenum shows spontaneous rhythmic contractions due to intrinsic pacemaker activity. These contractions are modified by adrenoceptor agonists: α1-adrenoceptor activation increases frequency and amplitude (contraction), while β2-adrenoceptor activation decreases them (relaxation). Both adrenaline and noradrenaline can be distinguished by their relative effects on α vs β receptors.
Preparation: rabbit is killed by air embolism; 3–5 cm of duodenum is removed and mounted in Krebs solution at 37°C with 1 g tension and carbogen; equilibrate 30 min until spontaneous contractions are regular.
Bioassay: add adrenaline at 0.01–1 μg/mL. At low doses, β2 stimulation decreases amplitude; at higher doses, α1 stimulation increases it. Noradrenaline predominantly contracts (α1 >> β2 activity). By using selective blockers: add phentolamine (α-blocker) — only the relaxant (β2) response remains; add propranolol (β-blocker) — only the contractile (α1) response remains.
Uses: (1) distinguish α vs β adrenergic components of a drug; (2) screen for α1 or β2 activity of new compounds; (3) bioassay of adrenaline content in a sample by comparison with a standard adrenaline solution.
Reference drug: adrenaline (1 μg/mL) is used as standard. The potency of an unknown is estimated from the response ratio using the interpolation method.

questions.answer:
1. Histamine bioassay on guinea pig ileum:
(a) Preparation: 2–3 cm segment of terminal ileum from a guinea pig; mounted in Krebs solution at 37°C, 1 g tension, 95% O2/5% CO2.
(b) Response: contraction of longitudinal smooth muscle — graded, reproducible, proportional to histamine concentration over the range 1–1000 ng/mL.
(c) Receptor: H1; mediated through Gq/IP3/Ca2+ pathway.
(d) Confirmation: mepyramine (diphenhydramine, cetirizine) — H1 antagonist — completely abolishes the response; atropine does not affect it; this confirms H1 specificity.
(e) Standard curve: prepare standard histamine solutions (5, 10, 20, 50 ng/mL) in Krebs; record contraction heights; plot log-dose vs response; fit linear regression.
(f) Calculation: add unknown sample to bath; record response height; read off equivalent log-dose from the regression line; calculate concentration in the original sample using the dilution factor. Example: if 0.1 mL of sample added to a 25 mL bath produces a response equivalent to 20 ng histamine standard, the sample concentration = 20 ng / 0.1 mL = 200 ng/mL.
(g) Sensitivity: approximately 1 ng/mL; far more sensitive than chemical methods for histamine.
2. Serotonin (5-HT) bioassay on rat fundus strip:
(a) Preparation: longitudinal muscle strip from the fundus of a fasted rat; mounted in Krebs at 37°C, 0.5–1 g tension, carbogen.
(b) Response: contraction — graded, proportional to 5-HT concentration over 0.1–100 ng/mL.
(c) Receptor: primarily 5-HT2 (5-HT2A); mediated through Gq/IP3/Ca2+ pathway.
(d) Confirmation: ketanserin or methysergide (5-HT2 antagonists) block the response; mepyramine (H1 antagonist) and atropine do not affect it; phentolamine does not affect it. This distinguishes 5-HT from histamine, ACh and catecholamines.
(e) Standard curve: same approach as histamine; 5-HT 0.1–10 ng/mL plotted on log-dose axis.
(f) Calculation: same interpolation method as for histamine.
(g) Uses: bioassay of 5-HT in blood, biological extracts or preparations; screening of 5-HT2 antagonists; study of drugs affecting platelet 5-HT release.
3. Comparison: the guinea pig ileum responds to multiple autacoids (histamine, bradykinin, 5-HT, ACh, opioids) and requires selective antagonists to identify each. The rat fundus strip is relatively selective for 5-HT at low concentrations and is preferred when only 5-HT is to be assayed. For definitive identification of an unknown substance in a biological extract, the cascade superfusion system uses both preparations simultaneously with a panel of selective antagonists.

questions.answer:
1. In-vitro bioassay: performed on isolated tissue in an organ bath. The drug acts directly on the tissue without absorption, distribution or first-pass metabolism. Only one receptor type is involved (if the tissue is selected appropriately). Conditions (temperature, pH, ionic composition, O2) are fully controlled. Results are reproducible and variability is low. Examples: guinea pig ileum for histamine; rat fundus strip for 5-HT; rat uterus for oxytocin.
2. In-vivo bioassay: performed in an anaesthetised or conscious intact animal. The drug must be absorbed (unless given i.v.) and distributed to its target organ; it undergoes metabolism and excretion. The response reflects the integrated pharmacological effect including reflex cardiovascular and autonomic compensation. Variability is higher. Examples: cat blood pressure for histamine (fall in BP); rat blood pressure for angiotensin (rise in BP); dog thoracic duct lymph for hyaluronidase.
3. Comparison table:
   In-vitro: simple, controlled, selective, economical in animals, no ADME; misses systemic effects.
   In-vivo: complex, reflex compensation, high variability, more animals; captures whole-animal pharmacology.
4. Cascade superfusion: a technique in which the perfusate from a reservoir (or from an antigen-challenged tissue that releases autacoids) flows sequentially through a series of isolated tissue preparations in a cascade (like a waterfall).
5. Construction: Krebs solution (or biological sample) is pumped at a constant rate from a reservoir through a heating coil (to reach 37°C) and then flows over successive tissue preparations, each in its own open organ bath, before being discarded. The tissues are mounted in series.
6. Tissue sequence example: reservoir perfusate → rat fundus strip (selective for 5-HT) → guinea pig ileum (histamine, bradykinin, 5-HT, ACh) → rat colon (PGE2 relaxes, PGF2α contracts) → rat uterus (oxytocin).
7. Identification using antagonists: selective antagonists are superfused over individual tissues. If mepyramine over the ileum abolishes a contraction that persists in the fundus strip, the substance is histamine. If the same substance contracts the fundus strip (blocked by methysergide) but not the mepyramine-blocked ileum, it is 5-HT.
8. Applications: (a) release of autacoids from antigen-challenged guinea pig lung (Kellermeyer-Graham technique) — identifies which mediators are released during anaphylaxis; (b) pharmacological characterisation of an unknown autacoid; (c) simultaneous demonstration of multiple mediator releases in a single experiment without additional animals.
9. Advantages of cascade: each preparation is exposed to the same concentration of test substance simultaneously; no dilution or storage is needed; interaction between autacoids (e.g., histamine potentiating 5-HT) is detected; the method minimises the number of animals used (one animal provides four to five tissues for the cascade).
10. Limitations: requires a stable flow rate; tissues age at different rates; pharmacological interaction between substances is confounded; autacoid concentrations in the perfusate may fall below the detection threshold of the tissues if the sample is very dilute.
questions.question: Compare in-vitro and in-vivo bioassays. Describe the cascade superfusion technique and explain its use in simultaneous bioassay of multiple autacoids.

questions.answer:
1. Background: angiotensin I (Ang I) is a decapeptide generated from angiotensinogen by renin; it is converted by angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE, a zinc metallopeptidase) to angiotensin II (Ang II), an octapeptide. Ang II is 10–50 times more potent as a vasoconstrictor. Ang II acts on AT1 receptors on vascular smooth muscle to cause vasoconstriction and on the adrenal cortex to release aldosterone.
2. Preparation: Wistar or Sprague-Dawley rat (200–250 g) is anaesthetised with urethane (1.25 g/kg i.p.). The femoral vein is cannulated for injection. The common carotid artery is cannulated with a heparinised polyethylene catheter connected to a pressure transducer and amplifier. The trachea is intubated to maintain a patent airway.
3. Procedure: allow 15–20 min for stabilisation after surgery. Record resting mean arterial pressure (MAP). Inject Ang I or Ang II i.v. in doses of 10–300 ng/kg, allowing recovery to baseline between doses. Record the peak rise in MAP.
4. Response: both Ang I and Ang II produce a dose-related rise in blood pressure. Ang II produces a larger rise at the same dose (10–50× more potent) because it directly activates AT1 receptors. Ang I must first be converted to Ang II by ACE in the lung.
5. Distinguishing Ang I from Ang II: (a) administer captopril (ACE inhibitor, 1 mg/kg i.v.) and repeat the pressor test with Ang I — the response is markedly reduced or abolished, because conversion to Ang II is blocked. The Ang II response is unaffected by captopril (Ang II does not require ACE). (b) Administer losartan (AT1 antagonist) — it blocks both Ang I (via its conversion product Ang II) and Ang II. This distinguishes ACE inhibitors (block Ang I but not Ang II) from AT1 antagonists (block both).
6. Use in screening antihypertensives: captopril, enalapril or any ACE inhibitor can be screened by this method: a drug that abolishes the Ang I pressor response but not the Ang II response is an ACE inhibitor. A drug that abolishes both is an AT1 antagonist or a drug that blocks AT2 (which mediates vasodilation, so AT2 blockade would augment the pressor response — not seen with selective AT1 antagonists).
7. Bradykinin accumulation test: ACE also inactivates bradykinin. After captopril treatment, inject bradykinin — the vasodepressor response is enhanced (bradykinin is not destroyed). This test confirms ACE inhibition.
8. Blood pressure measurement: direct intra-arterial measurement gives continuous, accurate readings including systolic, diastolic and mean arterial pressure. The pressor response is quantified as the peak rise in MAP from baseline.
9. Limitations: anaesthesia suppresses baroreflex; the absolute blood pressure levels in the anaesthetised rat differ from the conscious state; drug distribution is faster i.v. than by any other route.
10. Calculation of potency: construct a log-dose vs pressor response curve for Ang I and Ang II; calculate pressor ED50 for each. Potency ratio = ED50(Ang I) / ED50(Ang II). After captopril, calculate the percentage inhibition of Ang I response = [(response without captopril - response with captopril) / response without captopril] × 100%.
questions.question: Describe the bioassay of angiotensin on rat blood pressure. How are angiotensin I and II distinguished? What is the role of ACE inhibitors and AT1 antagonists in this assay?

questions.answer:
ACh on frog heart: the isolated, spontaneously beating frog heart is perfused with frog Ringer. ACh (1–10 ng/mL) reduces the rate and amplitude of contractions through M2 muscarinic receptors — a negative chronotropic and inotropic response. Atropine (0.1 μg/mL) abolishes this response, confirming muscarinic mediation. This preparation is very sensitive to ACh and was historically used for bioassay; it is now mainly a teaching preparation to demonstrate muscarinic cardiac effects. Nicotine or tubocurarine have no effect on M2 receptors, confirming selectivity.
ACh on cat blood pressure: an anaesthetised cat receives ACh i.v. ACh first produces a fall in blood pressure (muscarinic vasodilation through M3 receptors on endothelium releasing nitric oxide, and direct vasodilation). After atropine (0.5 mg/kg i.v.) the muscarinic depressor response is abolished. A further dose of ACh now produces a rise in blood pressure — this is Dale's vasomotor reversal. The pressor response unmasked is due to ACh stimulating nicotinic receptors in sympathetic ganglia and the adrenal medulla, releasing catecholamines that increase cardiac output and vasoconstrict. It is also enhanced by ACh activating adrenal chromaffin cells via nicotinic receptors to release adrenaline.
Dale's vasomotor reversal significance: (1) demonstrates that ACh has both muscarinic (fall in BP) and nicotinic (rise in BP after atropine) effects in vivo; (2) classically illustrates the dual pharmacology of ACh and the concept of receptor selectivity; (3) the same preparation can be used to characterise selective muscarinic or nicotinic drugs.
questions.question: Describe the bioassay of acetylcholine on the frog heart and on cat blood pressure. What does Dale's vasomotor reversal demonstrate?

questions.answer:
Bradykinin bioassay:
Preparation: guinea pig ileum or rat uterus.
Receptor: bradykinin B2 receptor (Gi/Gq-linked).
Response on guinea pig ileum: contraction, slower onset and more sustained than histamine contraction. The contraction is not blocked by mepyramine or atropine; it is blocked by icatibant (a selective B2 receptor antagonist). This confirms B2 mediation.
Response on rat uterus: sustained tonic contraction; not blocked by atosiban (oxytocin antagonist), distinguishing it from oxytocin. Blocked by icatibant.
Concentration range: 0.1–100 ng/mL (less sensitive than the guinea pig ileum for histamine).
Prostaglandin bioassay:
Rat fundus strip: both PGE2 and PGF2α contract the rat fundus via EP3/EP1 and FP receptors respectively. The contraction is slower than 5-HT, is not blocked by methysergide or mepyramine, and is reduced by indomethacin (COX inhibitor if prostaglandins are formed in situ, though exogenously added prostaglandins are not affected). PGE2 and PGF2α are distinguished by the rat colon preparation: PGE2 relaxes the colon longitudinal muscle (EP2 receptor, cAMP), while PGF2α contracts it (FP receptor). This opposite directionality in the cascade allows the two to be identified simultaneously.
Used to study: NSAIDs (reduce endogenous prostaglandin formation, which can be measured by reduced baseline tone or response in inflammatory preparations), thromboxane synthesis inhibitors, and prostacyclin analogues.
questions.question: Explain the bioassay of bradykinin and prostaglandins on isolated tissues. Name the preparations, receptors involved and confirmation tests.

questions.answer:
Standard curve construction: dilute standard histamine (histamine dihydrochloride in Krebs solution) to give concentrations of 2, 5, 10, 20 and 50 ng/mL (covering the linear range 20–80% of maximum response). Add 0.1 mL of each concentration to a 10 mL bath. Record contraction height in mm after each dose; wash out before the next. Plot log(concentration ng/mL) on the x-axis vs response (mm) on the y-axis. Fit a linear regression:
Example data:
  2 ng/mL → 8 mm; 5 ng/mL → 13 mm; 10 ng/mL → 18 mm; 20 ng/mL → 24 mm; 50 ng/mL → 33 mm.
Regression line from the linear range (10–50 ng/mL, response 18–33 mm):
  Slope b = (33 - 18) / (log50 - log10) = 15 / (1.699 - 1.000) = 15 / 0.699 = 21.5 mm/log unit.
  Equation: Response = 18 + 21.5 × (log[C] - 1.000)
Test of unknown: a plasma ultrafiltrate (0.5 mL) added to the same 10 mL bath produces a response of 20 mm.
Calculation:
  From equation: 20 = 18 + 21.5 × (log[C] - 1.000)
  2 = 21.5 × (log[C] - 1.000)
  log[C] = 1.000 + 2/21.5 = 1.000 + 0.093 = 1.093
  Equivalent histamine concentration in bath = antilog(1.093) = 12.4 ng/mL
Concentration in bath = 12.4 ng/mL (bath volume 10 mL, so total histamine = 12.4 × 10 = 124 ng)
Volume of sample added = 0.5 mL, so concentration in original sample = 124 / 0.5 = 248 ng/mL.
