questions.answer:
Autacoids (Greek: autos = self, akos = remedy) are biologically active compounds produced locally in the tissues that act near their site of release. They are not classical hormones (which travel in the blood to distant targets), but they exert potent local regulatory effects.
Histamine: stored bound to heparin in mast cell granules and basophil granules; also in ECL cells of the gastric mucosa and histaminergic neurons of the hypothalamus. Released by IgE-mediated mast cell degranulation (anaphylaxis), physical stimuli (heat, cold) and chemicals (morphine, tubocurarine). Biosynthesis: L-histidine → (L-histidine decarboxylase) → histamine. Metabolism: diamine oxidase and histamine-N-methyltransferase.
Histamine receptors: H1 (Gq; smooth muscle, endothelium, sensory nerves, brain) — bronchoconstriction, vasodilation, oedema, itch, wakefulness. H2 (Gs; parietal cell, heart) — gastric acid secretion, tachycardia. H3 (Gi; presynaptic CNS) — autoreceptor, reduces histamine release. H4 (Gi; eosinophils, mast cells) — chemotaxis in inflammation.
5-Hydroxytryptamine (serotonin): synthesised from tryptophan by tryptophan hydroxylase and aromatic amino acid decarboxylase. Main stores: enterochromaffin cells of the GI tract (90% of body 5-HT), platelets (taken up from portal blood), raphe nuclei of the brainstem (central serotonergic neurons). Metabolism: MAO and aldehyde dehydrogenase → 5-hydroxyindoleacetic acid (5-HIAA) in urine.
5-HT receptors: 5-HT1 (Gi; CNS, vasculature) — vasoconstriction (sumatriptan). 5-HT2 (Gq; smooth muscle, platelets) — contraction, platelet aggregation. 5-HT3 (ion channel; GI, chemoreceptor trigger zone) — depolarisation, emesis, GI motility. 5-HT4 (Gs; GI tract) — promotes motility (metoclopramide partially, prucalopride fully).

questions.answer:
Biological medicines include insulin, heparin, oxytocin, vaccines, antibiotics (earlier), growth hormones, blood products and cytokines. For many of these, chemical analysis alone is insufficient to guarantee clinical potency because: (1) the molecule may be complex, heterogeneous or incompletely characterised (heparin is a polymer mixture); (2) chemical degradation products may be chemically similar but biologically inactive or toxic; (3) manufacturing changes may alter the three-dimensional structure (and hence biological activity) without changing the chemical composition.
Role of bioassay in standardisation: a WHO International Standard is established for each biological medicine; its potency in International Units is defined in a bioassay using the specific biological test for that substance. All subsequent batches are assigned potency by comparison with the International Standard in the same bioassay system. This guarantees that 1 IU of insulin from any manufacturer in any country produces the same blood glucose reduction in a rabbit.
Role in quality control: each batch of a biological medicine is released for clinical use only after passing its bioassay potency test. The 95% fiducial limits of the potency estimate must fall within the pharmacopoeial acceptance range (usually 80–120% or 80–125%). If a batch falls outside this range, it is rejected regardless of its chemical analysis result.
Examples: insulin bioassay on blood glucose in rabbits (now largely replaced by radioimmunoassay); heparin bioassay on clotting time; oxytocin bioassay on rat uterus; digitalis bioassay on frog heart (cardiac arrest method); vaccines — potency testing for polio and DPT by protection tests in animals (being progressively replaced by in-vitro immunological methods, 3Rs compliance).
questions.question: Describe the relevance of bioassay in drug standardisation and quality control of biological medicines.

questions.answer:
1. Acetic acid-induced writhing test (visceral analgesic screening):
Principle: intraperitoneal acetic acid (0.6%, 10 mL/kg) irritates the peritoneum and causes rhythmic abdominal contractions, flank drawing and hind limb extension (writhing). The mediators are prostaglandins and bradykinin released from the peritoneum.
Procedure: fast mice 18 h; drug or vehicle p.o. 30 min before acetic acid i.p.; count writhes for 20 min.
Endpoint: number of writhes; analgesic drugs reduce it.
Drugs detected: both opioids (morphine, pethidine) and NSAIDs (aspirin, indomethacin) are active. Morphine > aspirin in potency. Very sensitive but non-selective — many sedatives and anticonvulsants also reduce writhes.
2. Tail flick test (spinal thermal nociception):
Principle: radiant heat applied to the tail activates C and Aδ nociceptors; the tail flick is a spinal reflex with its centre in the dorsal horn.
Procedure: measure baseline latency (2–4 s); administer drug; measure latency at 15, 30, 60 min; use a cut-off time of 10 s.
Endpoint: tail flick latency; opioids increase it.
Drugs detected: centrally acting analgesics, primarily opioids; NSAIDs are largely inactive. The model is selective for opioids and cannot detect mild analgesics.
3. Hot plate test (supraspinal thermal nociception):
Principle: the mouse stands on a hot plate at 55°C; paw licking or jumping requires intact supraspinal pain processing.
Procedure: measure baseline latency (5–10 s for licking); drug; measure at 15, 30, 60 min; cut-off 60 s.
Endpoint: licking or jumping latency; opioids increase it; NSAIDs do not.
Drugs detected: centrally acting analgesics requiring an intact CNS. Used with the tail flick test to confirm supraspinal action.
4. Formalin test (neurogenic and inflammatory phases):
Principle: sub-plantar formalin (1–5%, 20 μL) produces two phases of pain behaviour. Phase 1 (0–5 min): direct C-fibre activation (neurogenic). Phase 2 (20–40 min): inflammatory, prostaglandin and bradykinin-mediated.
Procedure: inject formalin; count licking and biting time in Phase 1 and Phase 2 separately.
Endpoint: licking/biting time in each phase.
Drugs detected: Phase 1 — opioids only; Phase 2 — both opioids and NSAIDs. This test distinguishes neurogenic from inflammatory pain, making it more informative than the writhing test.
5. Randall-Selitto test (mechanical hyperalgesia):
Principle: a pressure is applied to an inflamed (carrageenan-treated) rat paw; the paw pressure threshold (PPT) is lowered by inflammation. Analgesics restore PPT.
Endpoint: PPT (g of pressure) at which the rat vocalises or withdraws; analgesics increase it.
Drugs detected: both opioids and NSAIDs; also useful for detecting central sensitisation drugs.
6. Comparison table:
Writhing: visceral pain; both opioids and NSAIDs; sensitive but non-selective.
Tail flick: spinal thermal; opioids mainly; selective for opioids; spinal mechanism.
Hot plate: supraspinal thermal; opioids; requires supraspinal integrity.
Formalin Phase 1: neurogenic; opioids only.
Formalin Phase 2: inflammatory; opioids and NSAIDs.
Randall-Selitto: mechanical hyperalgesia; both drug classes.
questions.question: Describe the animal models used in the screening of analgesic drugs. For each model, state the principle, procedure, endpoint, drugs detected and their comparison.

questions.answer:
1. Carrageenan-induced paw oedema (acute inflammation):
Principle: carrageenan (a sulphated polysaccharide) injected sub-plantar in the rat causes biphasic inflammatory oedema.
Phase 1 (0–1 h): release of histamine and 5-HT from local mast cells — controlled by antihistamines.
Phase 2 (1–3 h): prostaglandin (PGE2) production via COX pathway — controlled by NSAIDs.
Phase 3 (3–6 h): bradykinin, further prostaglandins, peak oedema.
Procedure: fast rat 18 h; inject drug or vehicle p.o. 30 min before carrageenan (1%, 0.1 mL) sub-plantar right hind paw; measure paw volume by water displacement plethysmometry at 0 (baseline), 1, 2, 3 and 4 h.
Endpoint: % oedema inhibition at 3 h = [(Vc - Vt) / Vc] × 100, where Vc = oedema in control, Vt = oedema in treated.
Reference drug: indomethacin 10 mg/kg or diclofenac 25 mg/kg p.o.
2. Cotton pellet granuloma (chronic inflammation — proliferative):
Principle: sterile cotton pellets implanted subcutaneously induce a foreign body granuloma over 7 days. The granuloma weight (dried pellet weight minus initial pellet weight) reflects transudate (fluid) in the first 3 days and granulation tissue (fibroblast proliferation, collagen) thereafter.
Procedure: implant two 10 mg cotton pellets subcutaneously under ether anaesthesia; administer drug daily for 7 days; remove and dry granulomas on day 8.
Endpoint: dry granuloma weight (mg). % inhibition = [(Wc - Wt) / Wc] × 100.
Reference drug: dexamethasone 0.5 mg/kg (inhibits both exudate and proliferation).
What is detected: NSAIDs mainly reduce the exudative phase (wet weight); corticosteroids also reduce the proliferative phase (dry weight).
3. Acetic acid peritonitis (leucocyte accumulation):
Principle: acetic acid i.p. triggers prostaglandin-mediated chemotaxis of neutrophils into the peritoneal cavity.
Procedure: drug or vehicle 30 min before acetic acid (1%, 10 mL/kg i.p.); sacrifice 4 h later; collect peritoneal lavage with PBS; count leucocytes (Neubauer haemocytometer or automated counter).
Endpoint: total and differential leucocyte count (neutrophils). % inhibition.
Reference drug: indomethacin 10 mg/kg.
4. Freund's complete adjuvant (CFA) arthritis (immune-mediated chronic inflammation):
Principle: CFA (Mycobacterium tuberculosis in mineral oil) injected into one hind paw triggers an immune response that produces systemic polyarthritis resembling rheumatoid arthritis at 14–21 days.
Primary lesion: injection site, days 0–5. Secondary lesion: contralateral paw and systemic joints, day 14–28 (T-cell mediated).
Procedure: single injection of CFA 0.1 mL into the plantar surface; measure paw volumes of primary and secondary paws weekly for 28 days; administer drug daily.
Endpoint: secondary paw volume (reflects immune-mediated component). Reference drug: methotrexate 2 mg/kg (DMARD).
NSAIDs mainly reduce the primary lesion; DMARDs reduce both but especially the secondary (immune) lesion.
questions.question: Describe the animal models used in screening anti-inflammatory drugs. For each model, state the principle, procedure, mediators involved, the endpoint and the reference drug.

questions.answer:
1. Sedatives and hypnotics:
(a) Actophotometer (locomotor activity): an actophotometer measures locomotor activity as the number of infrared beam interruptions per unit time. CNS stimulants increase counts; CNS depressants decrease them. Amphetamine (2.5 mg/kg) is the reference stimulant; pentobarbitone (35 mg/kg) is the reference depressant.
(b) Pentobarbitone sleeping time: mice receive a sub-hypnotic dose of pentobarbitone (35 mg/kg i.p.) that does not induce sleep alone. A prior dose of a CNS depressant augments it and induces sleep. Sleeping time is measured as the duration from loss of righting reflex to its recovery. Diazepam prolongs sleeping time (reference). Used for phenobarbitone, benzodiazepines, valproate.
(c) Rotarod: motor coordination test at 10–25 rpm; fall time decreases with sedation. Distinguishes sedation from anxiolysis.
2. Anxiolytics:
(a) Elevated plus maze: exploits innate fear of open spaces in rodents. Time in open arms increases with anxiolytics. Diazepam is the reference (1–2 mg/kg i.p.). 5-HT1A partial agonist buspirone also increases open arm time without impairing rotarod performance, confirming it is not simply sedating.
(b) Light-dark box: mouse moves between lit and dark compartments. Anxiolytic increases time in the lit box.
(c) Social interaction test: anxiety reduces active social contact time between unfamiliar rats; anxiolytics restore it.
3. Antidepressants:
(a) Forced swim test (Porsolt): mouse or rat in inescapable water cylinder; records immobility time. Antidepressants reduce immobility. TCAs (imipramine) and SSRIs (fluoxetine) both effective; also MAO inhibitors and SNRIs.
(b) Tail suspension test: mouse suspended by its tail; immobility time measured 6 min. Antidepressants reduce immobility. Same drug sensitivity as FST but no swimming confound. Not used in rats.
4. Antiepileptics:
(a) MES test: supramaximal electrical current (corneal electrodes) produces tonic-clonic seizures; abolition of tonic hind limb extension (THE) = protection. Predicts clinical activity against grand mal (generalised tonic-clonic) seizures. Active drugs: phenytoin, carbamazepine, lamotrigine, valproate, phenobarbitone. Inactive: ethosuximide.
(b) PTZ test: pentylenetetrazol (90 mg/kg i.p.) produces clonic convulsions; absence of clonics = protection. GABA-A channel blocker; predicts absence and myoclonic seizure activity. Active drugs: ethosuximide, valproate, benzodiazepines, gabapentin. Inactive: phenytoin and carbamazepine.
Comparison: a drug active in MES but not PTZ is likely a Na+ channel blocker; active in PTZ but not MES is likely a GABA enhancer or T-type Ca2+ channel blocker; active in both has a broad-spectrum profile (valproate, lamotrigine).
questions.question: Describe the animal models used for screening CNS drugs: (a) sedatives and hypnotics, (b) anxiolytics, (c) antidepressants, and (d) antiepileptics.

questions.answer:
Model: carrageenan is injected sub-plantar (0.1 mL of 1% solution in saline) into the right hind paw of a rat. It is a biphasic (sometimes described as triphasic) inflammatory reaction caused by the sequential release of different inflammatory mediators.
Phase 1 (0–1 hour): immediate release of histamine and 5-HT from local mast cells activated by the mechanical and chemical stimulus. H1 antihistamines and anti-5-HT drugs reduce this phase. NSAIDs have minimal effect here.
Phase 2 (1–3 hours): production of prostaglandins (PGE2, PGI2) via inducible COX-2 and constitutive COX-1. This is the phase most sensitive to NSAIDs and COX inhibitors. The 3-hour time point is therefore used for anti-inflammatory screening with NSAIDs.
Phase 3 (3–6 hours): bradykinin, further prostaglandins, neutrophil accumulation; peak oedema. Corticosteroids suppress this phase most effectively.
Measurement: paw volume is measured by water displacement plethysmometry at baseline (0 h) and at 1, 2, 3 and 4 hours. Oedema volume = measured volume − baseline. % inhibition = [(oedema control − oedema treated) / oedema control] × 100.
Reference drug: indomethacin 10 mg/kg or diclofenac 25 mg/kg p.o., reducing 3-hour oedema by 50–60% in the standard model.
Use: widely used for initial screening of potential anti-inflammatory drugs; NSAIDs, corticosteroids and novel COX-2 inhibitors are evaluated in this model before clinical development.
questions.question: Describe the carrageenan-induced paw oedema model of acute inflammation. What mediators are involved at each phase and what does the model screen for?

questions.answer:
Principle: the EPM exploits the natural conflict between the exploratory drive of rodents and their innate fear of open, elevated, brightly lit areas. Anxious animals display thigmotaxis (a preference for enclosed, dark areas). An anxiolytic drug reduces this fear and allows the animal to spend more time in the open, exposed arms.
Apparatus: a plus (+) shaped elevated platform, 50 cm above the floor. Two arms are open (no walls) and two are enclosed (with 15 cm high walls). All arms are 30 cm long and 5 cm wide. The whole apparatus is in a dimly lit room to minimise the difference between open and closed arm brightness.
Procedure: place the mouse or rat at the central junction facing one open arm; record behaviour for 5 minutes using a video tracking system or direct observation. Animal is not startled or disturbed.
Parameters measured:
(1) Time in open arms (% of total time): the primary anxiolytic endpoint. Anxiolytics increase open arm time; anxiogens decrease it.
(2) Open arm entries (% of total entries): a secondary endpoint. An entry is counted when all four paws enter an arm.
(3) Total arm entries: a measure of general locomotor activity (anxiety-independent). An anxiolytic should not decrease total entries significantly — if it does, sedation is confounding the result.
(4) Time in closed arms: should decrease with anxiolytics.
Reference drugs: diazepam 1 mg/kg i.p. increases open arm time and entries significantly. Caffeine (anxiogen) decreases open arm time. Buspirone (5-HT1A partial agonist) increases open arm time without reducing total entries, confirming it is not sedating.
Limitation: the test is used only once per animal (the anxiety response habituates on second exposure); it does not distinguish between reduced anxiety and reduced fear memory consolidation.
questions.question: Describe the elevated plus maze (EPM) test for anxiolytic activity. What is the principle and what does each parameter measure?

questions.answer:
MES (maximal electroshock seizure) test:
Procedure: supramaximal electrical current (50 mA, 60 Hz, 0.2 s, sine wave) is delivered through corneal electrodes coated in saline to mice (or rats). The resulting seizure progresses: tonic flexion → tonic extension of hindlimbs → clonic convulsions → postictal depression.
Endpoint: protection is defined as abolition of tonic hind limb extension (THE). A protected animal shows only clonic movements or no convulsions at all.
Clinical prediction: predicts activity against generalised tonic-clonic seizures (grand mal) and partial seizures. The mechanism screened is primarily voltage-gated Na+ channel blockade.
Active drugs: phenytoin, carbamazepine, lamotrigine, valproate, phenobarbitone, oxcarbazepine.
Inactive: ethosuximide.
PTZ (pentylenetetrazol) test:
Procedure: pentylenetetrazol (PTZ, 85–90 mg/kg i.p. for mice) is injected; animals are observed for 30 minutes. PTZ blocks the GABA-A receptor chloride channel, reducing GABAergic inhibition.
Endpoint: protection is defined as abolition of clonic convulsions (whole-body jerking). A CD97 dose of protective drug prevents clonics in 97% of animals.
Clinical prediction: predicts activity against absence seizures (petit mal) and myoclonic seizures. The mechanism screened is enhancement of GABA-A inhibition or T-type Ca2+ channel blockade.
Active drugs: ethosuximide (T-type Ca2+ channel blocker), valproate, benzodiazepines, gabapentin.
Inactive: phenytoin, carbamazepine.
Comparison and clinical significance: a drug active in MES but not PTZ (phenytoin, carbamazepine) is likely a Na+ channel blocker used for partial and tonic-clonic seizures; active in PTZ but not MES (ethosuximide) predicts absence seizure activity. Broad-spectrum drugs (valproate, lamotrigine) are active in both tests.
questions.question: Describe the MES and PTZ tests for antiepileptic activity. How do they predict different clinical seizure types?

questions.answer:
Forced swim test (Porsolt despair test):
Principle: when placed in a cylinder of water from which it cannot escape, a mouse or rat initially swims vigorously, then adopts an immobile floating posture (passive floating). This immobility is termed behavioural despair, proposed as a model of depression-like helplessness.
Procedure: mice are placed in a glass cylinder (10 cm diameter, 25 cm water height, 25°C) for 6 minutes. Rats use a larger cylinder (20 cm diameter, water 30 cm, 25°C) for 15 minutes. A forced pre-swim is done 24 h before the test to establish a stable immobility baseline. Immobility is scored (seconds) in the last 4 min for mice, last 5 min for rats.
Endpoint: immobility time; antidepressants reduce it.
Reference drugs: imipramine (TCA, 10–30 mg/kg i.p.), fluoxetine (SSRI, 10 mg/kg i.p.), venlafaxine (SNRI).
Tail suspension test (TST):
Principle: a mouse is suspended by its tail from a horizontal rod for 6 min. It initially struggles to escape, then adopts passive immobility.
Procedure: the mouse's tail is taped to a horizontal rod 50 cm above the bench. Immobility in the last 4 min is recorded (automated or visual scoring).
Endpoint: immobility time; antidepressants reduce it.
Reference drug: imipramine (15–20 mg/kg), fluoxetine (10 mg/kg).
Comparison:
FST: used in both mice and rats; swimming can be a locomotor confound; cold water affects behaviour; more widely validated.
TST: used only in mice (rats climb their own tails); no swimming variable; easier to automate; tail climbing is a confound.
Both tests share the same drug sensitivity profile for TCAs, SSRIs, SNRIs and MAO inhibitors, but are insensitive to antipsychotics and benzodiazepines at non-sedating doses.
questions.question: Describe the forced swim test (FST) and tail suspension test (TST) for antidepressant screening. Compare the two models and name the reference drugs.

questions.answer:
Principle: a small volume of dilute formalin (1–5%, 20–50 μL) injected into the dorsal surface of the mouse hind paw causes two distinct phases of nociceptive behaviour:
Phase 1 (0–5 minutes): direct chemical stimulation of nociceptors — primary afferent C fibres are depolarised by formaldehyde, triggering a neurogenic (non-inflammatory) pain response.
Phase 2 (20–40 minutes): a quiescent interphase (5–20 min) is followed by an inflammatory phase in which bradykinin, prostaglandins, 5-HT and substance P are released from damaged tissue. Spinal sensitisation (wind-up) also contributes.
Endpoint: the mouse licks, bites or holds up the injected paw. The cumulative time spent licking/biting in Phase 1 and Phase 2 is recorded separately (automated video analysis or visual scoring at 5-min intervals).
Phase 1 drug sensitivity:
Opioids (morphine, pethidine): active, because they block C-fibre transmission at the spinal dorsal horn.
NSAIDs: largely inactive in Phase 1, because there is minimal prostaglandin production at this early time.
Phase 2 drug sensitivity:
Opioids: active.
NSAIDs (aspirin, ibuprofen, diclofenac): active, because prostaglandins drive Phase 2.
COX-2 selective inhibitors: active in Phase 2 only.
Significance: the formalin test is considered more clinically predictive than the hot plate or tail flick test because it involves two distinct pain mechanisms and mirrors clinical pain conditions (e.g., articular pain has both a neurogenic and inflammatory component). It detects both strong and mild analgesics at appropriate doses, and it characterises the mechanism of action by comparing Phase 1 and Phase 2 activities.
questions.question: Describe the formalin test of analgesia. How does it distinguish neurogenic from inflammatory pain, and which analgesic drugs are active in each phase?

questions.answer:
1. Purpose of toxicity studies: toxicity testing characterises the harm a new chemical entity can cause, determines safe dose levels, identifies target organs for toxicity, and provides data for first-in-human dose selection.
2. Acute toxicity — LD50 by Lorke's method:
   Stage 1: 3 mice per group are given the test substance at three doses spanning three orders of magnitude (10, 100 and 1000 mg/kg). Observe for 24 h; record deaths.
   Stage 2: based on Stage 1 results, four doses in the range containing the LD50 are chosen; 1 animal per dose is used. Observe 24 h.
   Calculation: LD50 = √(highest zero-mortality dose × lowest 100% mortality dose). Example: if 300 mg/kg → 0 deaths, 600 mg/kg → 1/1 deaths, then LD50 = √(300 × 600) = 424 mg/kg.
   Limit test: if no deaths occur at 2000 mg/kg (or 5000 mg/kg per OECD 423/425), the LD50 exceeds the limit and the substance is classified as practically non-toxic (GHS Category 5).
   Clinical signs recorded: body weight, food and water intake, motor activity, posture, respiration, skin, mucous membranes, eye signs; gross necropsy at 14 days.
3. Sub-acute toxicity (28-day study, OECD 407, ICH S4):
   Species: Wistar or Sprague-Dawley rats and one non-rodent (usually dog).
   Doses: three dose levels (low, mid, high) + vehicle control; 10 animals/sex/group.
   Parameters: (a) Body weight and food/water intake — weekly. (b) Ophthalmology — before and at study end. (c) Clinical pathology (haematology: CBC, differential, platelets; clinical biochemistry: liver enzymes ALT/AST, ALP, creatinine, electrolytes, glucose, bilirubin; urinalysis: volume, pH, glucose, protein, casts) — weeks 2 and 4. (d) Organ weights: liver, kidney, spleen, heart, adrenal, thyroid, gonads, brain — absolute and relative to body weight. (e) Gross pathology of all organs. (f) Histopathology of all major organs, minimum: liver, kidney, heart, lung, spleen, thyroid, adrenal, gonads, GI tract, bone marrow, brain. All at high dose and controls; targeted organs at other doses.
   NOAEL (No Observed Adverse Effect Level): the highest dose at which no statistically or biologically significant adverse finding is detected in any measured parameter. The NOAEL is the basis for calculating the maximum recommended starting dose (MRSD) for the first-in-human Phase I study: MRSD = NOAEL × (body surface area or body weight conversion factor) / safety factor (typically 10 for interspecies uncertainty in rodent studies; can be adjusted based on toxicokinetics).
4. Genotoxicity studies (ICH S2(R1)):
   (a) Ames test (bacterial reverse mutation): Salmonella typhimurium strains auxotrophic for histidine are exposed to the test chemical ± rat liver S9 fraction (for metabolic activation by CYP enzymes). A mutagen restores the ability to grow on histidine-free agar; colony count vs control is the endpoint. Positive = mutagenic. This test identifies base-pair substitution mutagens and frameshift mutagens.
   (b) Micronucleus test (in-vivo): mice receive the test substance; bone marrow is sampled at 24, 48 and 72 h; polychromatic erythrocytes (PCE) are stained and examined for micronuclei (chromosomal fragments or lagging chromosomes that failed to segregate). An increase in micronuclei in PCEs compared with normochromatic erythrocytes indicates clastogenic or aneugenic activity.
   (c) In-vitro chromosomal aberration test or mouse lymphoma assay: an additional in-vitro genotoxicity test of a mammalian cell.
5. Special toxicity:
   Reproductive toxicity (Segment II, teratogenicity): drug given to pregnant rats during organogenesis (day 6–15); dams examined at day 20; foetuses examined for external, visceral and skeletal malformations.
   Chronic toxicity and carcinogenicity: 6–24 months in rodents; complete histopathological examination of all major organs; tumour incidence reported.

1. Study design: male Wistar rats (200–250 g), 6 per route. IV group receives a bolus dose (e.g., 5 mg/kg) into the femoral vein. Oral (PO) group receives 10 mg/kg by gavage. Cross-over design with a 7-day washout may be used if the drug's t½ is short.
2. Blood sampling: serial blood samples (200 μL) from the jugular cannula or tail vein. Typical time points (oral): pre-dose, 0.25, 0.5, 1, 2, 4, 6, 8, 12 and 24 h. IV: pre-dose, 0.083 (5 min), 0.25, 0.5, 1, 2, 4, 8 and 24 h.
3. Sample processing: centrifuge at 3000 rpm for 10 min; collect plasma; store at -80°C until analysis by validated HPLC-UV or LC-MS/MS.
4. AUC by the linear trapezoidal method: each consecutive pair of time points forms a trapezoid with area = [(Ci + Ci+1)/2] × (ti+1 - ti). Sum all trapezoids from t = 0 to t = last measurable concentration.
5. Terminal extrapolation: from the last three to five time points, fit log(C) vs t by linear regression; slope = -λz/2.303; λz = terminal elimination rate constant. AUC(tlast → ∞) = Clast / λz. Total AUC(0 → ∞) = AUC(0 → tlast) + Clast/λz.
6. Worked PK parameters:
   Cmax and Tmax: read directly from the PO plasma concentration-time profile.
   t½ = 0.693 / λz.
   CL (total body clearance from IV data) = Dose(IV) / AUC(0→∞)(IV).
   Vd (volume of distribution) = CL / λz, or equivalently = Dose(IV) / (AUC × λz).
   Bioavailability F = [AUC(PO)/Dose(PO)] / [AUC(IV)/Dose(IV)] × 100%.
7. Example calculation:
   IV dose = 5 mg/kg; AUC(IV) = 2000 ng·h/mL; λz = 0.139 h-1
   CL = 5000 μg/kg / 2000 ng·h/mL = 2.5 L/h/kg (after unit conversion)
   t½ = 0.693 / 0.139 = 5 h
   Vd = 2.5 / 0.139 = 18 L/kg
   PO dose = 10 mg/kg; AUC(PO) = 2400 ng·h/mL
   F = [2400/10] / [2000/5] × 100% = 240 / 400 × 100% = 60%
8. Allometric scaling: physiological parameters scale with body weight (BW) according to power functions across species.
   CL(human) = CL(rat) × (BW_human / BW_rat)^0.75
   Example: CL(rat) = 2.5 L/h/kg × 0.25 kg = 0.625 L/h
   CL(human, 70 kg) = 0.625 × (70/0.25)^0.75 = 0.625 × (280)^0.75 ≈ 0.625 × 85 = 53 L/h ≈ 0.76 L/h/kg
   Vd scales as (BW)^1.0 (directly proportional). This gives Vd(human) = Vd(rat, L/kg) × 70 kg.
9. The allometric prediction provides a first estimate of human PK parameters for designing Phase I dosing regimens; it is refined by human in-vitro data (microsomal clearance, plasma protein binding) and confirmed in Phase I clinical trials.
10. IVIVC (in-vitro-in-vivo correlation): a Level A IVIVC establishes a point-to-point relationship between the in-vitro dissolution rate and the in-vivo absorption rate for a modified-release dosage form. If a validated Level A IVIVC exists, the FDA allows in-vitro dissolution to serve as a surrogate for a human bioequivalence study for certain formulation changes.

questions.answer:
1. Target identification and validation: a molecular target (enzyme, receptor, ion channel, transporter) is identified from genetic, biochemical or clinical evidence. Validation confirms that modulating the target produces the desired therapeutic effect in a relevant cell-based or animal model. Experimental pharmacology: in-vitro receptor binding assays, isolated tissue experiments to confirm functional activity at the target.
2. Hit identification: large chemical libraries are screened against the validated target using high-throughput screening (HTS; robot-driven plate assays) or virtual screening (computational docking). Hits are compounds that show activity above a threshold in the primary assay. Experimental pharmacology: concentration-response assays, selectivity panels.
3. Lead identification: hits are confirmed in dose-response experiments (IC50/EC50), tested for selectivity against related targets, and assessed for drug-like properties (Lipinski's rule of 5: MW ≤ 500, logP ≤ 5, H-bond donors ≤ 5, H-bond acceptors ≤ 10). Experimental pharmacology: in-vitro efficacy, selectivity and preliminary ADME (solubility, Caco-2 permeability, microsomal stability).
4. Lead optimisation: medicinal chemists modify the lead to improve potency, selectivity, metabolic stability, oral bioavailability and to reduce toxicity (hERG inhibition, genotoxicity). Experimental pharmacology: iterative cycles of synthesis, in-vitro testing and in-vivo PK in mice/rats.
5. Preclinical development package: (a) Pharmacology: in-vitro efficacy (IC50), in-vivo efficacy in relevant animal disease model (confirms therapeutic hypothesis), safety pharmacology (cardiovascular, CNS, respiratory — ICH S7A/S7B). (b) ADME: metabolic pathways (CYP, UGT identification), plasma protein binding, tissue distribution, excretion routes. (c) Toxicology: acute toxicity (LD50), 28-day sub-acute toxicity (NOAEL), genotoxicity (Ames test, micronucleus), reproductive toxicity if applicable.
6. IND (Investigational New Drug) filing: submitted to the regulator (CDSCO in India, FDA in the USA, EMA in Europe). Includes: pharmacology summary, ADME summary, toxicology summary, proposed clinical protocol, investigator qualifications, GMP manufacturing data for the clinical batch.
7. Phase I clinical trial: 20–80 healthy volunteers (or patients for oncology drugs); single ascending dose (SAD) followed by multiple ascending dose (MAD) studies; objectives: safety, tolerability, human PK parameters, dose range for Phase II. First-in-human dose derived from NOAEL in animals.
8. Phase II clinical trial: 100–300 patients; proof-of-concept; optimal dose selection; preliminary efficacy and safety. Randomised, controlled, usually double-blind.
9. Phase III clinical trial: 1000–3000 patients; large-scale comparison with standard therapy or placebo; pivotal efficacy and safety evidence for registration.
10. NDA/MAA filing and regulatory approval: the complete clinical and preclinical dossier is submitted; regulators review safety and efficacy data; approval or refusal issued.
11. Phase IV post-marketing surveillance: continued safety monitoring in a broader patient population; detection of rare adverse events (< 1:1000); pharmacovigilance; risk management plans. Experimental pharmacology remains involved: in-vitro mechanistic studies to explain emerging safety signals, animal models to test drug interactions, PK/PD modelling to support dose adjustments in special populations.

Lorke's method is a staged acute toxicity test designed to minimise animal use while estimating the LD50 with acceptable precision.
Stage 1: three groups of 3 mice each receive 10, 100 and 1000 mg/kg. Observe for 24 hours.
Result here: 0 deaths at 10 and 100 mg/kg; 3/3 deaths at 1000 mg/kg. The LD50 lies between 100 and 1000 mg/kg.
Stage 2: choose four doses spanning this range (at approximately equal log intervals). One mouse per dose.
Result here: 150 → 0/1; 300 → 0/1; 600 → 1/1; 1200 → 1/1.
The transition from 0 deaths to 1 death occurs between 300 and 600 mg/kg.
Identify:
  Highest dose with zero mortality = 300 mg/kg (D0)
  Lowest dose with 100% mortality = 600 mg/kg (D1)
Calculation: LD50 = √(D0 × D1) = √(300 × 600) = √180000 = 424 mg/kg
Total animals used: 9 (Stage 1) + 4 (Stage 2) = 13 mice — far fewer than the classical 50-animal method.
Significance: the LD50 estimates the acute hazard of the compound. Combined with the No Effect Level and the therapeutic ED50, it gives the therapeutic index (LD50 / ED50). Lorke's method complies with the 3Rs (Reduction) principle because it uses the minimum number of animals needed to determine the LD50 range. The result guides the selection of dose levels for sub-acute toxicity studies (the high dose in a 28-day study is usually 1/10 to 1/5 of the LD50).

The International Council for Harmonisation (ICH) S-series guidelines standardise the preclinical toxicity studies required before clinical trials and regulatory approval of new drugs across the USA, EU and Japan.
ICH S1 (Carcinogenicity studies): S1A defines when carcinogenicity studies are needed (drugs for chronic use, genotoxic signals); S1B describes the standard 2-year rodent carcinogenicity bioassay design; S1C gives guidance on dose selection.
ICH S2(R1) (Genotoxicity): requires a standard battery including a bacterial reverse mutation test (Ames test), an in-vitro chromosomal aberration test or mouse lymphoma assay, and an in-vivo micronucleus or chromosomal aberration test. All three must be conducted before Phase II trials.
ICH S3 (Toxicokinetics): S3A describes how toxicokinetic data (exposure measurements in animals at toxicological doses) are used to interpret toxicity studies; S3B covers pharmacokinetics in repeat-dose toxicity studies.
ICH S4 (Single and repeat-dose toxicity): S4A sets the duration of chronic toxicity studies in rodents and non-rodents needed to support clinical trials of different lengths. A 28-day study supports Phase I; a 90-day study supports Phase II; a 6-month rodent study supports chronic clinical use.
ICH S5 (Reproductive and developmental toxicity): segment I (fertility), segment II (embryo-foetal development = teratogenicity), segment III (peri- and post-natal). Required before Phase III for drugs taken by women of childbearing potential.
ICH S6 (Biotechnology-derived pharmaceuticals): adapted toxicology approaches for biologicals (monoclonal antibodies, proteins) where standard small-molecule approaches may not apply.
ICH S7A and S7B (Safety pharmacology): S7A requires evaluation of effects on cardiovascular, CNS and respiratory systems at pharmacological doses before first-in-human trials; S7B specifically addresses the risk of QT interval prolongation (hERG assay, in-vivo telemetry).

The pithed rat preparation was first described by Gillespie and Muir (1967). It is an in-vivo cardiovascular preparation in which the brain and spinal cord have been destroyed (pithing), leaving the cardiovascular system intact.
Procedure: a Wistar rat is lightly anaesthetised with ether. A metal rod (pithing rod) is introduced through the orbit, pierces the skull, and is advanced through the spinal canal to destroy the spinal cord. The animal is immediately placed on artificial ventilation (tracheal cannula, rodent ventilator, 60–70 breaths/min, 10 mL/kg tidal volume). The carotid artery is cannulated for direct blood pressure monitoring; the femoral vein is cannulated for drug injection. All CNS-mediated cardiovascular reflexes are abolished (baroreceptor reflex, chemoreceptor reflex, vasomotor centre).
Uses:
1. Determination of direct vascular effects of drugs without baroreflex confound: a drug that raises blood pressure in an intact anaesthetised rat also elicits reflex bradycardia; in the pithed rat the pressure rise is seen without the reflex component, so the pure vascular effect is quantified.
2. Adrenoceptor subtype characterisation: catecholamines administered to the pithed rat produce cardiovascular responses that can be precisely blocked by selective antagonists (e.g., the pressor response to phenylephrine is abolished by prazosin, confirming α1-adrenoceptor mediation; the positive chronotropic response to isoprenaline is abolished by propranolol, confirming β1-adrenoceptor mediation).
3. Screening of sympathomimetics: compounds can be tested for their direct agonist activity at alpha and beta adrenoceptors without the confounding variable of central sympathetic activation.
4. Comparison with intact anaesthetised preparation: the same drug is tested in both preparations; differences between the responses reveal the contribution of baroreflexes to the in-vivo blood pressure response.

The Shay rat ulcer model (1945) uses pyloric ligation to study gastric secretion and screen anti-ulcer drugs.
Principle: ligation of the pylorus prevents emptying of gastric secretions; acid and pepsin accumulate in the stomach over 4 hours, eventually causing back-diffusion of acid into the mucosa and an acute stress ulcer. The model measures both ulcer formation (Shay's original use) and total gastric acid output (the main use today for antiulcer drug screening).
Procedure: fast rats for 24 hours (water allowed until 2 hours before surgery); anaesthetise with urethane (1.25 g/kg i.p.) or pentobarbitone (40 mg/kg i.p.); make a mid-line incision; identify the pylorus and ligate it tightly with a silk thread; administer the test drug intragastrically (via a polyethylene tube through the mouth to the stomach body) or intraduodenally; close the abdomen; allow 4 hours; re-anaesthetise if needed; sacrifice the animal; collect gastric juice by cutting the lower oesophagus and emptying the stomach through the pylorus.
Measurements:
(a) Volume of gastric juice (mL) — reduced by proton pump inhibitors, H2 blockers.
(b) Total acidity by titration with 0.01N NaOH (meq/L); total acid output = volume × acidity (meq/4 h).
(c) Free acid (titratable to pH 3.5) and total acid (to pH 7.0) may be reported separately.
(d) pH of gastric juice.
(e) Pepsin activity (optional): by casein digestion.
Reference drugs and expected results:
Omeprazole (10 mg/kg i.g.): 90%+ reduction in total acid output (irreversible H+/K+-ATPase block).
Ranitidine (50 mg/kg i.p.): ~70% reduction (H2 blockade).
Sucralfate (500 mg/kg i.g.): reduces ulcer index but minimal effect on acid output (cytoprotective).
Antacids: raise pH but do not reduce acid output.
Ulcer index (gross pathology): scored on a 0–5 scale based on number, size and depth of mucosal lesions seen when the stomach is opened and stained with carmine red.

# Unit 1: Principles and Ethics of Bioassay

Experimental pharmacology uses living systems — isolated tissues, whole animals or even microorganisms — to measure the potency of a drug or biological substance. This unit covers the logic of bioassay, the statistical machinery behind it, and the ethical framework that governs work with animals.

## 1.1 Definition and concept of bioassay

A **bioassay** (biological assay) is a procedure that uses a living organism or its components to estimate the potency or concentration of a substance by comparing its effect with that of a reference standard. It is used when the substance is chemically undefined, structurally heterogeneous, or when its pharmacological activity cannot be predicted from its chemical composition alone.

**Advantages over chemical assay**
- Measures the actual biological activity, not just the chemical quantity present.
- Detects unknown impurities that alter biological effect but are chemically identical.
- Useful for heterogeneous mixtures such as insulin, digitalis or heparin.
- Required for substances whose structure is incompletely known.

**Limitations**
- Greater biological variability than a chemical measurement.
- Requires living systems that must be maintained under strict, standardised conditions.
- Results can vary with the species, age, sex, strain and physiological state of the animal or tissue.
- More expensive and time-consuming than physicochemical assays.
- Ethical constraints limit use of animals.

## 1.2 Types of bioassay by nature of the response

### Quantal (all-or-none) bioassay
The response is binary: either an event occurs or it does not. Examples: death or survival, convulsion or none, sleep or wakefulness, oedema or none. The endpoint is the **proportion of animals showing the response** at each dose. Because each animal gives only one piece of information (yes or no), larger group sizes are needed.

### Graded bioassay
The response is measured on a continuous scale: height of a muscle contraction, change in blood pressure in mmHg, change in heart rate. Each animal or tissue can receive several doses, and the **degree** of response is measured against dose. Graded assays are more efficient because one preparation gives multiple data points.

| Feature | Quantal | Graded |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Response measured | Proportion responding | Magnitude of response |
| Data per subject | One observation | Multiple observations |
| Statistical endpoint | ED50, LD50 | Relative potency, Emax |
| Example | Sleeping time test, LD50 | Muscle bath, blood pressure |

## 1.3 Standard preparations and working standards

A **standard preparation** (or reference standard) is a stable, well-characterised preparation of the substance, adopted by a regulatory authority, against which test preparations are compared. Its potency is defined in **International Units (IU)** or **Units**.

A **working standard** is a secondary standard prepared and calibrated against the international or national standard within a laboratory. It is used for daily assays to avoid depleting the reference standard.

**WHO International Biological Standards** are maintained by the WHO Expert Committee on Biological Standardisation. Examples include:
- 1st IRP for Insulin (defined as 1 IU = 41.67 μg).
- International Standard for Heparin.
- International Standards for vaccines, antibiotics, blood products and cytokines.

**Units of biological activity** are defined empirically for each substance: one Unit of insulin lowers blood glucose in a rabbit by a specified amount under defined conditions; one Unit of heparin prolongs the clotting time of sheep plasma under specified conditions. The numerical value of one Unit is arbitrary and historical.

## 1.4 Dose-response curves

### Log-dose vs response (semi-logarithmic plot)
When dose is plotted on a linear scale the relationship between dose and graded response is hyperbolic. When dose is replotted on a **logarithmic scale** the curve becomes sigmoidal (S-shaped), which has a linear region between about 20% and 80% of the maximum. This linear region is used for statistical analysis and for bioassay calculations.

### Emax model (rectangular hyperbola)
```text
Effect = Emax × [D] / (EC50 + [D])

Where:
  Emax = maximum achievable effect
  EC50 = concentration producing 50% of Emax
  [D]  = concentration of drug
```
This is a saturable, hyperbolic relationship. When [D] >> EC50 the effect approaches Emax; when [D] << EC50 the effect is proportional to [D] (linear pharmacology).

### Hill equation (sigmoidal Emax model)
```text
Effect = Emax × [D]^n / (EC50^n + [D]^n)

Where n = Hill coefficient (measure of cooperativity)
  n = 1 : simple hyperbola (Langmuir isotherm)
  n > 1 : sigmoidal, cooperativity (binding at one site facilitates the next)
  n < 1 : negative cooperativity
```

## 1.5 Methods of bioassay

### Matching assay (direct comparison method)
The unknown preparation is compared with the standard by finding doses of each that produce the **same response**. The response matched is typically mid-range (around 50% of Emax).

```text
Potency of unknown = (Dose of standard that matches) / (Dose of unknown that matches) × Potency of standard
```

Simple and quick; assumes linearity at the matched response level. Used where rapid results are needed and few data points are available.

### Interpolation assay
A calibration curve (log-dose vs response) is constructed with the standard. The response produced by an unknown dose is read off the curve to find the equivalent dose of standard. The potency of the unknown is then calculated from the ratio.

```text
If 10 units standard gives the same response as 0.5 mL unknown → 1 mL unknown = 20 units
```

### Bracketing assay (two-point, two-dose assay)
Two doses of standard (d1 and d2) **bracket** the response of the unknown. The relationship between log-dose and response is assumed to be linear in this range.

```text
Example:
  d1 (standard, 2 units) → response r1 = 20 mm
  d2 (standard, 4 units) → response r2 = 32 mm
  Unknown dose d_u    → response r_u = 26 mm
  By interpolation: log(potency) = log(d1) + (r_u - r1)/(r2 - r1) × (log d2 - log d1)
```

### Three-point assay
Uses three doses of standard (or two doses of standard and one of unknown) to construct the linear portion of the log-dose response curve. More precise than bracketing because it checks linearity. Commonly used for bioassay of acetylcholine on frog rectus abdominis.

### Four-point assay (parallel-line assay)
Two doses each of the **standard (S1, S2)** and the **unknown (U1, U2)** are used. Doses are chosen so that S1:S2 = U1:U2 (the same dose ratio). The two log-dose response lines must be **parallel** (a validity test) and must not cross. The horizontal distance between the two parallel lines is the **log-potency ratio** (M).

```text
Potency ratio R = antilog(M)
Potency of unknown = R × potency of standard per unit dose

Validity tests for a four-point parallel-line assay:
1. Parallelism: the two lines must be parallel (no significant slope difference).
2. Linearity: each line must be straight (no significant departure from linearity).
3. No significant difference in blank responses.
```

## 1.6 Statistical analysis

### ED50 and LD50 by probit analysis
For quantal data, the **probit** (probability unit) transformation converts sigmoidal cumulative frequency curves to straight lines.

```text
Probit = 5 + (z), where z is the z-score corresponding to the proportion responding
  Proportion 0.50 → probit 5.0
  Proportion 0.84 → probit 6.0
  Proportion 0.16 → probit 4.0
```
Probit vs log-dose gives a straight line. The log-dose corresponding to probit 5 (50% response) is the **ED50 (effective dose 50%)** or **LD50 (lethal dose 50%)**, depending on the endpoint.

### Moving averages method (Thompson 1947)
Used when the dose spacing is uniform on a log scale. The LD50 is estimated directly from the number of responses at each dose without full probit transformation. Simpler but less informative than probit analysis.

### Dixon and Mood method (up-and-down method)
Used when the number of animals is small. The first animal receives a dose near the expected LD50. If it survives, the next dose is raised by a fixed step; if it dies, the next dose is lowered. The LD50 is the geometric mean of doses at the transition points. Very economical in animal use.

## 1.7 Precision and validity

### Index of precision (λ)
```text
λ = s / b

Where:
  s = standard deviation of the log-dose response line about the regression
  b = slope of the line
```
A lower λ means a more precise assay. λ < 0.1 is excellent; λ > 0.2 is poor. Precision improves with more observations and a steeper, less variable response.

### Limits of error
The **fiducial limits** (confidence limits) of the estimated potency are calculated from the variance of the potency estimate. Typically the 95% fiducial limits are reported: the potency ratio lies within these limits with 95% probability.

### Validity tests for parallel-line assays
Four validity tests are assessed by analysis of variance (ANOVA) of the assay data:
1. **Preparations**: the two mean response levels (standard vs unknown) should not differ significantly from zero.
2. **Regression**: the slope (b) must be significant; a flat line gives no information.
3. **Parallelism**: the difference in slopes of the two lines must not be significant.
4. **Deviation from linearity (non-linearity)**: the response must not deviate significantly from a straight line.

If parallelism or linearity fail, the assay is invalid and must be redesigned.

## 1.8 Ethics in experimental pharmacology: the 3Rs

The 3Rs framework was proposed by Russell and Burch (1959) in "The Principles of Humane Experimental Technique" and is the foundation of modern animal ethics in research.

### Replacement
Finding methods that **avoid or replace** the use of animals. Full replacement substitutes cell culture, computer models, organ-on-a-chip, in-silico pharmacokinetic models or physicochemical tests for the animal. Partial replacement uses lower organisms (insects, fish larvae) instead of mammals.

Examples: Limulus amoebocyte lysate (LAL) test replaced the rabbit pyrogen test; human cell-based assays replaced animal bioassays for many cytokines; QSAR models predict toxicity without animals.

### Reduction
Using **fewer animals** to obtain the same quality of information. Strategies include better statistical design (fewer but informative group sizes), sharing tissues and control groups between studies, using in-vitro data to narrow the dose range before in-vivo work, and systematic reviews to avoid repeating experiments.

### Refinement
Modifying procedures to **minimise pain, suffering, distress and lasting harm** in animals that must still be used. Examples: use of local anaesthesia or analgesia, the choice of less invasive routes of administration, training animals to cooperate with procedures, use of humane endpoints, environmental enrichment, and housing in compatible social groups.

## 1.9 CPCSEA guidelines (India)

The **Committee for the Purpose of Control and Supervision of Experiments on Animals (CPCSEA)** operates under the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals Act, 1960.

**Key requirements:**
- Every institution using animals must register with CPCSEA.
- An **Institutional Animal Ethics Committee (IAEC)** must be constituted. It must include a veterinarian, a scientist in charge of animal care, a biological scientist, a scientist using animals, a nominee of the institutional head, and two nominees from CPCSEA (one of whom must be a person concerned with animal welfare outside the institution).
- All protocols involving animals must be reviewed and approved by the IAEC before the work begins.
- Animals must be housed in species-appropriate facilities with adequate space, bedding, environmental enrichment, food, water and a 12:12 light-dark cycle.
- Transport, procurement and anaesthesia must comply with prescribed standards.
- A veterinarian must be available to the facility.

**Humane endpoints** are criteria that allow early termination of a study when the animal shows signs of severe pain, distress or moribund condition, before death occurs. Examples: weight loss exceeding 20%, laboured breathing, inability to reach food or water, persistent prostration. Using humane endpoints is both more ethical and scientifically more informative than death as the endpoint.

## 1.10 Species and strain selection

The choice of animal for a pharmacological experiment depends on:
- **Pharmacological appropriateness**: the target organ, receptor or pathway must be present and functional in the species. For example, guinea pigs show strong bronchoconstriction with histamine (H1 receptors in bronchial muscle), making them suitable for anti-asthmatic screening; rats are preferred for cardiovascular work.
- **Body weight and size**: larger animals provide more tissue and blood but are more expensive and require larger doses.
- **Breeding history**: inbred strains are genetically homogeneous and reduce biological variability (Wistar and Sprague-Dawley rats, Swiss albino and C57BL/6 mice). Outbred stocks are more representative of human genetic diversity.
- **Regulatory requirements**: ICH guidelines specify species for toxicity studies.

## 1.11 Randomisation and blinding

**Randomisation** assigns animals to treatment groups by a random process (random number tables, computer-generated sequences), so that systematic bias in group allocation is eliminated. All known and unknown confounding factors are, on average, balanced between groups.

**Blinding** (masking) prevents the investigator from knowing which treatment a specific animal has received, which removes unconscious measurement bias. Single blinding is when the animal handler does not know the treatment; double blinding is when both the handler and the person scoring the results do not know.

## 1.12 Study design considerations

**Parallel design**: each animal receives one treatment only. Groups of animals are run simultaneously. Variability comes from between-animal differences. Requires more animals but is preferred when treatments have long carry-over effects.

**Crossover design**: each animal receives every treatment in sequence, acting as its own control. Variability is reduced because between-animal differences cancel out. Requires fewer animals. Valid only when treatments do not permanently alter the animal and when washout periods between treatments are adequate.

**Latin square design**: a crossover design for multiple treatments and multiple periods, balanced so that each treatment appears once in each row (animal) and each column (period). Removes both animal-to-animal and period-to-period variation from the error term.

```text
Latin square example (3 treatments: S, U, V; 3 periods; 3 animals):
         Period 1    Period 2    Period 3
Animal 1    S           U           V
Animal 2    U           V           S
Animal 3    V           S           U
```

## Remember

1. Bioassay measures biological activity by comparison with a standard; it is used when chemistry alone cannot determine potency.
2. Quantal assays count the proportion showing an all-or-none response; graded assays measure the magnitude on a continuous scale.
3. The log-dose vs response curve is linear between 20% and 80% of maximum; this linear region is used for calculations.
4. Four-point parallel-line assay uses two doses each of standard and unknown; validity requires parallelism and linearity.
5. Probit 5.0 = 50% response = ED50 or LD50; probit analysis converts the sigmoidal quantal curve to a straight line.
6. Index of precision λ = s/b; lower is better; λ < 0.1 is excellent.
7. 3Rs: Replacement = no animals at all; Reduction = fewer animals; Refinement = less suffering.
8. CPCSEA requires institutional registration and an IAEC that approves every protocol before work begins.
9. Use humane endpoints; never use death as the routine endpoint when alternatives exist.
10. Randomisation removes allocation bias; blinding removes measurement bias.

# Unit 2: Isolated Tissue Bioassays

Isolated tissue preparations allow the pharmacologist to study a drug's effect on a single tissue or receptor type, free from the integrating influences of the whole animal: reflexes, counter-regulatory hormones and metabolism by other organs are all excluded. This unit covers the technical basis of the organ bath, the tissues most commonly used and the calculations for each type of bioassay.

## 2.1 Principle of isolated tissue preparations

When a tissue is removed from the body and kept in a nutrient solution at the correct temperature with continuous oxygen supply, it retains its pharmacological responsiveness for one to several hours. Drugs added to this bathing solution diffuse into the tissue and produce measurable effects: a change in the tension of a muscle preparation is the most common endpoint.

The **signal** (usually isometric or isotonic muscle tension) is converted by a **transducer** to an electrical signal, amplified and recorded on a chart recorder or a data-acquisition computer. The resulting trace is an objective, permanent record of the response.

## 2.2 The organ bath

### Components and design

```text
Organ bath cross-section:

  Gas inlet (95% O2 / 5% CO2 or 100% O2) ───► bubbles through Krebs solution
  Jacketed outer chamber ─── thermostated water maintains 37°C (or species-specific temp)
  Inner bath ─── contains Krebs-Henseleit solution (25–75 mL)
  Tissue suspended vertically between two hooks
    Lower hook ── fixed to base
    Upper hook ── connected to isometric force transducer via thread
  Drug inlet ── usually by syringe into the bath
  Drain tap ── for rapid washout
```

### Types of organ baths
- **Simple organ bath**: a single-walled glass cylinder, temperature maintained by immersion in a water bath. Adequate for routine work.
- **Trendelenburg bath**: a U-shaped or angled bath in which the tissue is stretched longitudinally; used for intestinal preparations.
- **Jacketed organ bath**: double-walled; thermostated water circulates in the jacket. Maintains temperature precisely. The standard design for most modern work.

### Krebs-Henseleit solution composition (approximate, in mmol/L)

| Ion / Compound | Concentration (mmol/L) |
| --- | --- |
| NaCl | 118 |
| KCl | 4.7 |
| CaCl2 | 2.5 |
| MgSO4 | 1.2 |
| KH2PO4 | 1.2 |
| NaHCO3 | 25 |
| Glucose | 11 |

Purpose: provides the osmotic environment, ionic gradients and metabolic substrate identical to interstitial fluid. The bicarbonate/CO2 buffer (gassed with 95% O2 / 5% CO2) keeps pH at 7.4.

**Oxygenation**: continuous bubbling of carbogen (95% O2 / 5% CO2) supplies oxygen and removes carbon dioxide. The carbonate/bicarbonate buffer prevents the pH from drifting. Without adequate oxygenation, tissues lose contractility within minutes.

**Temperature control**: most mammalian tissues are studied at 37°C; frog tissues at 25°C or room temperature.

### Transducers
An **isometric force transducer** measures the change in tension when the muscle length is held constant (more common and more reproducible). An **isotonic transducer** measures the change in length when the load is held constant (used for recording lever movements). Modern preparations almost universally use isometric transducers with a computerised data acquisition system.

## 2.3 Commonly used isolated tissue preparations

### Frog rectus abdominis muscle

| Feature | Detail |
| --- | --- |
| Species | Frog (Rana tigrina or Rana hexadactyla) |
| Tissue | Rectus abdominis muscle strip |
| Receptor | Nicotinic acetylcholine receptor (N-M type) |
| Response | Contraction (increase in tension) |
| Medium | Frog Ringer's solution at 25°C |
| Uses | Bioassay of acetylcholine and other nicotinic agonists; study of neuromuscular blocking agents |

Atropine does not block the contraction in this preparation, confirming it is a nicotinic response. Tubocurarine blocks it competitively.

### Guinea pig ileum

| Feature | Detail |
| --- | --- |
| Species | Guinea pig (Cavia porcellus) |
| Tissue | 2–3 cm segment of ileum |
| Receptors | H1 (histamine), Kinin B2 (bradykinin), 5-HT3 (serotonin), μ-opioid, muscarinic |
| Response | Contraction |
| Medium | Krebs solution at 37°C, 95% O2 / 5% CO2 |
| Uses | Bioassay of histamine (most sensitive preparation); bradykinin, serotonin, opioid (naloxone-reversible relaxation); Schultz-Dale reaction for anaphylaxis |

The guinea pig ileum is the **most versatile and widely used isolated preparation**. Because it responds to so many autacoids it can be used in a cascade system to identify unknown substances.

**Schultz-Dale reaction**: an actively sensitised guinea pig ileum contracts violently when challenged with the specific antigen (antigen-antibody reaction on mast cells releases histamine and other mediators within the wall of the gut).

### Rabbit duodenum

| Feature | Detail |
| --- | --- |
| Species | Rabbit |
| Tissue | 3–5 cm segment of duodenum |
| Receptors | α1-adrenergic (contraction), β2-adrenergic (relaxation) |
| Response | Spontaneous rhythmic contractions that increase with α-agonists and decrease with β-agonists |
| Medium | Krebs solution at 37°C |
| Uses | Bioassay of adrenaline and noradrenaline; demonstration of α/β-adrenoceptor activities |

Adrenaline at low doses may first inhibit (β2 predominant at low concentrations), then stimulate (α1 predominant at higher concentrations) spontaneous contractions. Noradrenaline predominantly contracts. Phentolamine blocks the contractile component; propranolol blocks the relaxant component.

### Rabbit jejunum

| Feature | Detail |
| --- | --- |
| Species | Rabbit |
| Tissue | 3–5 cm segment of jejunum |
| Receptors | Oxytocin receptor (smooth muscle), prostaglandin TP receptor |
| Response | Contraction |
| Uses | Bioassay of oxytocin; prostaglandin bioassay (PGE2 relaxes, PGF2α contracts) |

### Rat uterus (oestrogen-sensitised)

| Feature | Detail |
| --- | --- |
| Species | Rat in oestrus or primed with oestrogen |
| Tissue | Uterine horn |
| Receptors | Oxytocin receptor, PGF2α receptor, oestrogen-sensitised smooth muscle |
| Response | Phasic contractions (frequency and amplitude) |
| Medium | De Jalon solution (a low-calcium Ringer) at 30°C |
| Uses | Bioassay of oxytocin (most sensitive preparation; used for WHO oxytocin standardisation); ergometrine; prostaglandins |

Oestrogen priming upregulates oxytocin receptors and increases the sensitivity of the uterus to oxytocin.

## 2.4 Experimental procedure for an isolated tissue bioassay

```text
Step 1: Sacrifice the animal humanely; remove the tissue immediately.
Step 2: Place tissue in cold, oxygenated Krebs solution to minimise hypoxic damage.
Step 3: Trim the tissue to the required size (avoid crushing the ends used for hooks).
Step 4: Mount the tissue in the organ bath; attach to fixed hook below and transducer thread above.
Step 5: Apply a resting tension (preload) appropriate to the tissue:
         - Guinea pig ileum: 0.5–1 g tension
         - Rat uterus: 0.5 g
         - Frog rectus: 0.2 g
Step 6: Equilibrate for 30–60 minutes in Krebs at 37°C with continuous oxygenation.
Step 7: During equilibration, wash the bath at intervals (every 15 min) with fresh Krebs.
Step 8: Confirm viability: add a reference agonist (e.g., histamine 10 ng/mL) and check for a reproducible contraction.
Step 9: Wash out and allow tension to return to baseline.
Step 10: Carry out the bioassay.
```

## 2.5 Cumulative dose-response curves

In a cumulative (non-equilibrium) concentration-response experiment, increasing concentrations of an agonist are added to the bath **without washing between doses**, so the agonist accumulates until a maximum response is reached. The logarithm of the concentration is plotted on the x-axis and the response (expressed as a percentage of maximum) on the y-axis. This gives a sigmoidal curve from which EC50 and Emax are read.

For the **classical bioassay**, non-cumulative dose-response is used: each dose is washed out completely before the next is added.

**Washing between doses**: at least two or three complete volume changes of fresh Krebs solution are needed to wash out a drug. Inadequate washing leaves residual agonist and shifts the baseline upward.

## 2.6 Bioassay of acetylcholine on frog rectus abdominis (three-point assay worked example)

The **three-point assay** uses three doses in a cycle: low dose of standard (S1), unknown (U), high dose of standard (S2), then S1 again. The sequence SUSSUS or S1US2S1US2 is repeated three or more times.

```text
Worked example:
  S1 = 10 ng ACh → mean contraction = 15 mm
  U  = volume V of unknown → mean contraction = 22 mm
  S2 = 40 ng ACh → mean contraction = 32 mm

  The linear log-dose response equation between S1 and S2:
    log(10) = 1.000  → response 15 mm
    log(40) = 1.602  → response 32 mm
    Slope b = (32 - 15) / (1.602 - 1.000) = 17 / 0.602 = 28.24 mm per log unit

  Log-dose for unknown (from interpolation on the line):
    Log(dose_U) = 1.000 + (22 - 15) / 28.24 = 1.000 + 0.248 = 1.248
    Dose of standard equivalent to U = antilog(1.248) = 17.7 ng

  If V = 0.1 mL was added:
    Concentration of ACh in unknown = 17.7 ng / 0.1 mL = 177 ng/mL
```

## 2.7 Bioassay of histamine on guinea pig ileum (bracketing method)

Standard histamine doses bracket the response of the unknown sample.

```text
Doses:    S_low = 20 ng/mL → response 15 mm
          Unknown U        → response 24 mm
          S_high = 80 ng/mL → response 36 mm

Log-dose for unknown:
  Log(20) = 1.301; Log(80) = 1.903
  b = (36 - 15) / (1.903 - 1.301) = 21 / 0.602 = 34.9 mm per log unit
  Log(dose_U) = 1.301 + (24 - 15) / 34.9 = 1.301 + 0.258 = 1.559
  Dose equivalent = antilog(1.559) = 36.2 ng/mL

This is the potency of the unknown expressed as ng histamine per mL.
```

## 2.8 Bioassay of oxytocin on rat uterus

The rat uterus responds to oxytocin with rhythmic contractions. The response measured is usually the **height of the contraction** in mm, or the **area under the tension-time curve** per unit time.

A calibration curve is constructed with 0.5, 1 and 2 mIU/mL oxytocin (using the International Standard). The unknown preparation is tested in the same range, and its potency in mIU/mL is read from the calibration curve by interpolation.

## 2.9 Estimation of pA2 (Schild plot) for competitive antagonists

The **pA2** is the negative logarithm of the molar concentration of an antagonist that requires a **doubling** of agonist concentration to produce the original response. It is a measure of antagonist potency.

**Procedure**:
1. Construct an agonist concentration-response curve without antagonist → note EC50 (call it D).
2. Add a fixed concentration of antagonist, allow equilibration, then repeat the agonist CRC → note the new EC50 (call it D').
3. Calculate the dose ratio r = D' / D.
4. Repeat for at least three antagonist concentrations (B).

**Schild equation**:
```text
log(r - 1) = log(B) - pA2

Plotting log(r - 1) vs log(B) gives a straight line with slope 1 and y-intercept = -pA2.
```
If the slope is exactly 1, the antagonism is competitive and reversible (Schild equation is satisfied). pA2 is then the x-intercept of the Schild plot.

## 2.10 Four-point parallel-line assay: matching bioassay calculation

```text
Standard doses: S1 = 10 units, S2 = 30 units (dose ratio = 3)
Unknown doses:  U1, U2 with the same dose ratio of 3

Mean responses:
  S1 → 18 mm, S2 → 30 mm
  U1 → 24 mm, U2 → 36 mm

Slope of standard line: b_S = (30 - 18) / (log30 - log10) = 12 / 0.477 = 25.16 mm per log unit
Slope of unknown line:  b_U = (36 - 24) / (log ratio)  = 12 / 0.477 = 25.16 (parallel, good)

Mean log-dose of standard: (log10 + log30)/2 = (1.000 + 1.477)/2 = 1.238
Mean response of standard: (18 + 30)/2 = 24 mm

Mean log-dose of unknown:  (logU1 + logU2)/2 = midpoint of unknown
Mean response of unknown:  (24 + 36)/2 = 30 mm

Log-potency ratio M = (mean response_U - mean response_S) / b_average
                    = (30 - 24) / 25.16 = 0.238

Potency ratio R = antilog(0.238) = 1.73

If the unknown was labelled as 10 units/mL, the true potency = 10 × 1.73 = 17.3 units/mL.
```

## Remember

1. The organ bath maintains the tissue in oxygenated Krebs at 37°C; NaHCO3 is the buffer, glucose is the substrate.
2. The frog rectus abdominis tests nicotinic ACh receptors; atropine does not block but tubocurarine does.
3. The guinea pig ileum is the most versatile preparation — it responds to histamine, bradykinin, 5-HT and opioids.
4. The oestrogen-sensitised rat uterus is the standard preparation for oxytocin bioassay.
5. Wash the bath thoroughly between doses; residual agonist gives falsely high baselines.
6. In the three-point assay cycle SUSU, interpolate the unknown response on the standard log-dose line.
7. The four-point parallel-line assay is valid only if the two lines are parallel and linear.
8. pA2 = -log(molar concentration of antagonist that doubles the agonist EC50); higher pA2 = more potent antagonist.
9. A Schild slope of 1 confirms competitive (reversible) antagonism.
10. Equilibrate the tissue for at least 30 minutes before starting the bioassay.
